title: Sein und Zeit — Interaktive Einführung
category_reason: German interactive introduction to Heidegger's 'Being and Time' (1927): Dasein, being-in-the-world, authenticity vs. inauthenticity, temporality as the horizon of Being. Pure phenomenological philosophy, no AI/ML content.
thesis: A German-language interactive introduction to Heidegger's 'Sein und Zeit': the question of the meaning of Being (Seinsfrage) is approached through the analysis of Dasein (the being for whom Being is an issue), whose fundamental structure is being-in-the-world (In-der-Welt-sein) — not a subject inside a container of objects, but an engaged, practical involvement with equipment (Zuhandenheit) that only breaks down in the moment of concern (Sorge).
key_claims: The 'Seinsfrage' (question of Being) asks not 'what is?' (which is answered by ontology/categorization) but 'what does it mean to be?' — the meaning of Being is temporality (Zeitlichkeit).

Dasein is the being that we ourselves are; its defining feature is that it is 'being-its-Own-most-Possibility' (seine eigentümste Möglichkeit) — it is always ahead of itself, already in a world, and being-alongside entities.

The primary way Dasein encounters entities is not theoretical observation but practical use (Zuhandenheit, 'readiness-to-hand'): the hammer is encountered as 'for hammering', not as an object with properties; the theoretical attitude (Vorhandenheit, 'presence-at-hand') is a derived mode.

Dasein is normally 'fallen' (verfallen) into the They (das Man): it interprets itself through public, average interpretations rather than its own authentic possibilities; authenticity (Eigentlichkeit) requires facing one's own Being-towards-death (Sein-zum-Tode).

Temporality is not clock-time but the ecstatical-horizonal structure of care (Sorge): Dasein is always already projected into the future (Sein-vor-zu), factually situated in the past (Geworfenheit, 'thrownness'), and present in the moment (Geworfenheit in der Gegenwart). The 'circle of temporality' (temporal circle) is the structure in which past, present, and future are not sequential but co-constitutive.
methods_math: hermeneutic circle: understanding is always circular (pre-structure of understanding)
ontological distinction: ontic (facts about beings) vs. ontological (the meaning of Being)
structural analysis: Dasein's existence is analyzed as care (Sorge) = being-ahead-of-itself + being-already-in + being-alongside
temporality as the meaning of Being: ecstases (future/past/present) as co-original
visualizations: interactive 'Dasein structure' diagram: three overlapping circles (ahead-of-itself / already-in / being-alongside) with the user able to 'collapse' one to see how the structure breaks down

Zuhandenheit vs. Vorhandenheit toggle: a hammer shown as 'for hammering' (transparent, integrated into the activity) vs. 'present-at-hand' (opaque object with properties); the toggle simulates the 'breakdown' (Störfall) that reveals the referential totality
temporality circle: a non-linear diagram where past, present, and future are three 'ecstases' pointing at each other; the user can rotate the diagram to see that no one is 'first'

das Man vs. Eigentlichkeit slider: a narrative scenario (e.g., 'you are deciding whether to take a risky job') where the slider shifts the decision from 'what everyone does' (das Man) to 'what I, facing my own death, choose' (authentic)
internal_tensions: The interactive format (sliders, toggles) is somewhat at odds with Heidegger's insistence that Dasein's structure must be 'lived' and cannot be reduced to a diagram; the visualizations risk making the existential structures look like mechanical parts.

The page presents 'Sein und Zeit' as a finished system, but Heidegger himself later (in the 'turn', Kehre) distanced himself from the work, and the interpretation of Dasein's temporality remains contested among Heidegger scholars.

title: Alan Watts — The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (Interaktive Konzeptvisualisierung)
category_reason: Philosophie/Psychologie: interaktive Konzept-Visualisierung von Alan Watts' Buch 'The Book: on the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are' (Ego, Selbstbild, Selbstwissen). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Watts' 'The Book' behauptet, dass das menschliche Ego ein Selbstbild (ein mentales Modell des 'Ich') ist, das wir mit dem eigentlichen Selbst verwechseln; das 'Tabu' ist, dass es gesellschaftlich geahndet wird, dieses Selbstbild abzulegen bzw. wahrzunehmen, wer man wirklich ist — dass man nicht ein abgegrenztes Ego, sondern der ganze Prozess ist. Die interaktive Konzept-Map macht die Kernideen (Ego, Selbstbild, Selbstwissen, Bewusstsein, Tabu) als vernetzte Knoten erfahrbar.
key_claims: Das Ego ist ein Selbstbild — ein mentales Modell des 'Ich', das wir fälschlich für das reale Selbst halten.
Selbstwissen ist im gewöhnlichen Sinn unmöglich: wie ein Auge, das sich nicht selbst sehen kann, kann das Bewusstsein nicht auf sich selbst 'blicken', ohne ein (falsches) Bild zu erzeugen.
Das 'Tabu gegen zu wissen, wer du bist' ist eine soziale Norm: Wer aus dem zugewiesenen Selbstbild ausbricht, wird sozial bestraft — das Tabu hält das Ego am Leben.
Das 'Selbst' ist ein Prozess, nicht eine Sache: Du bist der Vorgang (Atmen, Denken, Reagieren), nicht das Produkt.
Die Trennung zwischen 'ich' und 'Welt' ist eine Illusion, die vom Ego-Bild erzeugt wird; die Wirklichkeit ist ein ungeteilter Fluss.
Bewusstsein wird als 'Raum' beschrieben, in dem Gedanken erscheinen — nicht als der Inhalt, sondern als das Feld.
methods_math: Selbst-Referenz-Problem (das Auge, das sich nicht sieht)
visualizations: Plotly: interaktives Konzept-Netz (Begriffsknoten, klickbar, Hover-Details)
konzeptionelle Karten der Kernideen (Ego, Selbstbild, Tabu, Prozess, Raum)
internal_tensions: Watts' Ideen sind bewusst anti-systematisch und paradox; sie in ein starres Konzept-Netz zu gießen, erzeugt genau die Struktur, die das Buch verweigert.
Die zentralen Behauptungen (keines festen Selbst, Ego als Illusion) sind nicht 'visualisierbar' — die Netz-Karte ist eine didaktische Vereinfachung, keine Darstellung der Argumentation.
Die Unterscheidung 'Prozess vs. Objekt' wird behauptet, aber die epistemische Schwierigkeit (wie kann der Prozess sich als Prozess erkennen?) wird nur gestreift.

title: Weinherstellung — Interaktive Erkundung der Weinkelche
category_reason: An interactive German guide to winemaking chemistry: fermentation biochemistry, acid-base chemistry, sulfur dioxide, tannin polymerization, malolactic conversion, and aging. Pure food/organic chemistry with no AI or ML content.
thesis: An interactive German-language walkthrough of winemaking as applied chemistry: how yeast convert sugar to ethanol via glycolysis and alcoholic fermentation, how SO2 dosing works as redox chemistry, how tannins polymerize and astringe, and how malolactic fermentation shifts the acid profile — each section pairing a chemical equation with a slider or animation.
key_claims: Alcoholic fermentation is anaerobic glycolysis followed by decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetaldehyde and its reduction to ethanol; the net yield is 2 C6H12O6 -> 4 C2H5OH + 4 CO2, and only ~5% of the sugar energy is captured as ATP.

Sulfur dioxide acts as both a reductant (protecting wine from oxidation by preferentially binding O2) and a biocide (inactivating aldehyde oxidases in yeast cell walls); effective free-SO2 targets depend on total SO2, pH, and wine type.

Tannins are hydrolysable or condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins) whose astringency arises from precipitation of salivary proline-rich proteins; polymerization degree controls the perceived 'mouthfeel'.
Malolactic fermentation (MLF) is a bacterial decarboxylation of L-malic acid (2-hydroxybutanedioic acid) to L-lactic acid + CO2, raising pH by ~0.3 units and reducing harshness.
Esters (ethyl acetate, isoamyl acetate, etc.) formed during fermentation are the primary contributors to fruity aroma; their profile depends on yeast strain, temperature, and oxygen availability.
Browning (enzymatic and non-enzymatic Maillard) is the main aging degradation pathway; phenolic oxidation by polyphenol oxidase is the dominant enzymatic route in white wines.
methods_math: pH and buffer capacity (Henderson-Hasselbalch for tartaric/malic acid systems)
reaction kinetics (first-order degradation models for SO2, browning)
polymerization degree and its relation to molecular weight distribution
Le Chatelier's principle for fermentation equilibrium
visualizations: interactive fermentation pathway diagram with animated carbon flow from glucose to ethanol/CO2
SO2 speciation slider showing the free-bound equilibrium as a function of pH and temperature
tannin polymerization chain builder: click to add catechin units, watch molecular weight and astringency index grow
malic-to-lactic acid structure animation with the decarboxylation step highlighted
ester formation rate plot vs. temperature and yeast strain selection
browning colorimetry: visual wine color shift over simulated months with SO2 level as a control
internal_tensions: The guide treats winemaking as deterministic chemistry (stoichiometry, kinetics) while real winemaking is heavily empirical and strain-dependent; the interactive sliders give a false sense of predictive precision.
SO2 dosing is presented as a simple redox problem, but in practice the optimal free-SO2 level is a regulatory and sensory compromise, not a purely chemical optimum.
The MLF section is presented as a clean bacterial conversion, but in winemaking it is often a race against malolactic bacteria contamination and must be managed, not simply 'triggered'.

title: Was das Froschauge dem Froschhirn sagt — Lettvin et al. 1959
category_reason: German explanation of the classic Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch & Pitts (1959) paper on the frog's retina: electrophysiological identification of four types of retinal ganglion cells as 'feature detectors' (spot-on, spot-off, edge, moving-edge). Neuroscience / computational biology, no AI/ML focus (though the paper historically influenced early neural network work).
thesis: A German-language explanation of the landmark 1959 paper by Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch & Pitts: by recording from single retinal ganglion cells in the frog, they identified four cell types tuned to specific visual features (bright spot, dark spot, edge, moving edge), arguing that the frog's visual system is optimized for detecting flying-insect prey — a foundational result in computational neuroscience.
key_claims: The frog's retina contains four distinct types of retinal ganglion cells, each tuned to a different visual stimulus: 'spot-on' (bright blob), 'spot-off' (dark blob), 'edge' (light-dark boundary), and 'moving-edge' (directional motion).

The 'moving-edge' detector is the most behaviorally important: it fires only when a dark object moves against a bright background in a specific direction, which is exactly the signature of a flying insect against the sky.

The frog's visual system is not a general-purpose image processor but a highly specialized 'bug detector': the four cell types are sufficient for the frog's ecological niche (catching flying insects) and are not needed for tasks like reading or navigation.

The paper is a landmark in 'functional anatomy': it shows that the brain can be understood as a collection of specialized detectors, each solving a sub-problem, and that the overall behavior emerges from the combination of these detectors.

The McCulloch-Pitts neuron (a binary threshold unit) provides the theoretical framework: each ganglion cell can be modeled as a weighted sum of its inputs (from photoreceptors and bipolar cells) passed through a threshold, making the retina a 'wiring diagram' that can be analyzed logically.
methods_math: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model: binary threshold logic
direction selectivity as a temporal filter
visualizations: interactive receptive field diagram: a frog retinal ganglion cell's center-surround field with a movable light spot; the user can position the spot to see when each of the four cell types fires
moving-edge detector animation: a dark dot moves across a bright field; the 'moving-edge' cell fires only for the correct direction, with the firing rate shown as a live trace
comparison with human vision: the same stimulus shown to a 'human-like' visual system (with many more cell types) vs. the frog's four-cell system, highlighting the specialization trade-off
McCulloch-Pitts wiring diagram: the retinal circuit from photoreceptors through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, shown as a logical circuit with threshold gates
internal_tensions: The paper's 'four cell types' framing is an oversimplification: the frog's retina actually has more than four ganglion cell types, and the 'feature detector' interpretation has been refined by subsequent work; the page presents the 1959 result as the definitive picture.

The 'bug detector' interpretation is ecological but somewhat reductive: the same circuitry is used for other behaviors (startle response, orientation), and the four types are not the only information the frog's brain receives about the visual world.

title: Process & Reality — Interaktiv Erleben (A.N. Whitehead)

'Eternal objects' (colors, forms, math structures) are pure potentials that 'ingress' into concrete experiences.

title: Principal Bundles – Interaktives Lerntool

thesis: A principal bundle is a space carrying a full symmetry (Lie) group over each base point, and the real question is how those symmetries are globally twisted; that twist — the connection and its curvature — is exactly gauge physics (the EM potential, the field strength, and the Aharonov–Bohm effect).
key_claims: A Principal G-bundle has fiber = Lie group G acting freely and transitively on each fiber, base M = P/G, and is the 'mother bundle' from which every associated bundle P×_G F is built
A bundle is determined up to isomorphism by its transition functions g_ij satisfying the cocycle condition g_ij·g_jk·g_ki = e on triple overlaps
A connection is a 𝔤-valued 1-form ω; locally A_i = s_i*ω is the physics gauge potential, and curvature Ω = dω + ½[ω,ω] is the field strength
For U(1) electromagnetism the curvature F = dA is the EM field tensor, with gauge transformation A → A + ∂λ
Fundamental forces as connections: EM = U(1), weak = SU(2), strong QCD = SU(3) (8 gluons = dim su(3)), gravity = frame bundle with Lorentz group SO(3,1) and Riemann curvature
The Aharonov–Bohm effect: with F = 0 (flat connection) the holonomy exp(i∮A) = exp(iΦ/ℏ) can still be nontrivial — showing the gauge potential A, not only F, is physically real
Flat curvature (F = 0) does NOT imply a trivial bundle — holonomy can remain nontrivial

title: Spivak · Calculus on Manifolds — Interaktiv
category_reason: Pure differential-geometric/analytic exposition of Spivak's book (differential forms, Stokes, manifolds) with no AI/ML application; only points forward to de Rham cohomology and gauge-theory physics.
thesis: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, the Divergence theorem and Stokes' theorem are not four theorems but one (int_M dω = int_{∂M} ω) in four disguises; the proof is trivial (Fubini + 1D FTC) while the real work is in the definitions (alternating tensors, wedge, d, chains, ∂, orientation, manifolds, partition of unity).
key_claims: HDI, Green, Divergence and classical Stokes are a single statement ∫ dω = ∫_{∂} ω with different k and different ω; the classical notation (cross products, normal vectors) is just bookkeeping artifacts of ℝ³.
The proof of Stokes is 'a complete triviality' (three lines: Fubini + 1D fundamental theorem); the difficulty is entirely in the definitions — Spivak's own diagnosis from the preface.
The derivative is not a number but a linear map; Spivak's linear-approximation definition lives in every dimension, whereas the school formula fails because h is a vector and you cannot divide by it.
The determinant is the prototype of all differential forms: it is linear in each column and flips sign under column swap — the two properties that define alternating tensors.
d² = 0 (forms) and ∂² = 0 (chains) are the dual structures; Stokes' theorem says d and ∂ are adjoint with respect to the integral.
'Closed ⇒ exact' holds only on star-shaped regions (Poincaré lemma); dθ on ℝ²∖{0} is closed but not exact, so integrals detect holes — the beginning of topology.
On manifolds one must integrate forms, not functions, because forms carry the Jacobian factor |det| automatically under a change of chart (Satz 4-9).
Green, Divergence and classical Stokes are each obtained by choosing the right form ω of degree 0/1/2; rot grad f = 0 and div rot F = 0 fall out of d²=0 (Problem 4-19b).
methods_math: differential forms and exterior derivative d
n-dimensional Riemann integration, Lebesgue criterion (measure zero)
change of variables / Jacobian factor |det g'|
visualizations: Four-masks hero: one equation in four classical disguises (custom 2D canvas + Temml math)
Linear map / determinant-as-oriented-area, norm/open-set/boundary classifier, Riemann 2D upper/lower sums, measure-zero covering, Fubini slicing, change-of-variables (all custom 2D canvas)
Partition of unity, alternating-tensor and wedge-product demos, orientation/volume-element, 1-form and 2-form fields, d-operator and d²=0, dθ on ℝ²∖{0} (custom 2D canvas)
Chains and ∂²=0, step-through Stokes proof and a numerical live-verification of ∫dω = ∫_{∂}ω (custom 2D canvas)
Manifold 'locally flat', tangent space in 3D and Möbius band orientability (Plotly 3D surface / custom canvas)
Classical theorems (Green, Divergence in 3D, Stokes) numerically, Archimedes' principle as physics, and a dependency-graph of the book (custom 2D canvas + Plotly)
internal_tensions: The proof is trivial but the 'horde of difficult definitions' is the real content — the page is built to make those definitions tangible.
Whether 'closed ⇒ exact' holds depends on the topology (holes) of the region, not on the formula.
Area defined as a limit of inscribed triangles fails (Schwarz's cylinder); the correct definition is the integral over the volume element.
Partial derivatives alone do not imply differentiability — Satz 2-8 (continuous partials) is only sufficient, not necessary.

title: Was eine Mannigfaltigkeit ist — visuell erklärt
category_reason: Pure differential geometry education: a simplified visual explanation of manifolds, tangent spaces, and the generalized Stokes theorem (unifying HDI, Green, Divergence, Stokes) based on Spivak's 'Calculus on Manifolds'. No ML/AI focus.
thesis: A manifold is a space that is locally flat (like ℝⁿ) but globally curved; the generalized Stokes theorem ∫_M dω = ∫_∂M ω unifies the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, the divergence theorem, and the classical Stokes theorem into a single statement about any manifold with boundary.
key_claims: A manifold is locally flat, globally curved: every point has a neighborhood that smoothly deforms to a flat patch of ℝⁿ
Non-examples: cusps (no unique tangent), crossings (too many directions), self-intersections break the definition
The tangent space at a point is the unique direction the curve continues in — it rotates globally but is always 1D locally
HDI, Green, Divergence, and Stokes are all the same theorem in different dimensions/notations
The generalized Stokes theorem: ∫_M dω = ∫_∂M ω — the integral of the derivative over the interior equals the integral over the boundary
The hard work is in defining 'd' (exterior derivative) and 'ω' (differential form); once defined, all theorems follow

title: Catastrophe Theory Interactive Explorer
category_reason: Reine Mathematik/Dynamik: René Thoms Katastrophentheorie (Faltung, Schneide, Aalschwanz, Schmetterling; Hysterese; Bifurkationsmengen). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Die Katastrophentheorie (Thom) klassifiziert plötzliche, qualitative Zustandswechsel in Systemen, die von glatten Potentialfunktionen V(x; a,b,…) gesteuert werden: glatte Änderungen der Steuerparameter können ein Minimum verschwinden lassen, sodass das System springt – und für ≤2 Zustandsvariablen & ≤4 Steuerparameter gibt es exakt 7 elementare Katastrophen, von denen die vier Cuspoide (Faltung, Schneide, Aalschwanz, Schmetterling) hier interaktiv erkundet werden.
key_claims: Ein System mit Potential V(x; a,b,…) sitzt an Minima (stabile Gleichgewichte); eine glatte Parameteränderung kann ein Minimum auslöschen → plötzlicher Sprung ('Katastrophe').
Thoms Klassifikationssatz: für ≤2 Zustandsvariablen und ≤4 Steuerparameter existieren exakt 7 elementare Katastrophen (bis auf glatte Äquivalenz).
Die vier Cuspoide (1 Zustandsvariable): Faltung A₂ (V=x³+ax, 1 Parameter), Schneide A₃ (V=x⁴+ax²+bx, 2), Aalschwanz A₄ (V=x⁵+ax³+bx²+cx, 3), Schmetterling A₅ (V=x⁶+ax⁴+bx³+cx²+dx, 4).
Die Bifurkationsmenge der Schneide in (a,b)-Raum ist die Kurve 8a³+27b²=0; im Inneren koexistieren 2 stabile + 1 instabile Gleichgewichte (Bistabilität).
Hysterese: der Systemzustand hängt von der Geschichte ab – der Sweep der Steuerung macht bei Hin- und Rückweg an verschiedenen Werten; die eingeschlossene Fläche = dissipierte Energie.
Ball-on-Surface-Simulation: eine Kugel rollt per Gradientendurchlauf auf dem Potential und springt, wenn ihr aktuelles Minimum verschwindet.
Anwendungen: Phasenübergänge, Meinungsdynamik, Optik (Kaus­tiken), Triple-Übergänge.
visualizations: Plotly: Potential V(x) mit kritischen Punkten (alle 4 Cuspoide)
Plotly: Bifurkationsdiagramm (stabil/instabil)
Plotly 3D: Katastrophenfläche (Schneide)
Plotly: Bifurkationsmenge 8a³+27b²=0 (Schneide)
Canvas: Ball-on-Surface (Gradientendurchlauf)
Canvas: Phasenporträt (x, dx/dt)
Plotly: Hysterese-Schleife
Vergleichstabelle aller Cuspoide
internal_tensions: Die Katastrophentheorie wurde außerhalb der Mathematik (Biologie, Ökonomie) oft überdehnt; die Anwendungen hier sind korrekt, aber die 'Volkstheorie'-Kritik wird nicht thematisiert.
Nur die Cuspoide (1 Zustandsvariable) werden behandelt – die restlichen 3 elementaren Katastrophen (z.B. Elliptische, Hyperbolische Umbilic, Butterfly-Variationen) fehlen.
Die numerische Nullstellenfindung (Scan+Bisektion) ist robust, aber für 5/6-Gleichungen (Aalschwanz/Schmetterling) numerisch aufwendig – die Performance bei vielen Parametern bleibt unklar.

title: Christoffel Symbols — Visual Explorer
category_reason: English interactive explorer of Christoffel symbols on curved 2D surfaces: how the connection coefficients encode how a coordinate basis changes from point to point, with live 3D surface rendering and vector-field overlays. Pure Riemannian geometry.
thesis: An interactive English-language explorer that lets the user deform a 2D surface and watch the Christoffel symbols Γᵏᵢⱼ update in real time, showing how they measure the failure of the coordinate basis to be parallel, and how they enter the covariant derivative of a vector field on the surface.
key_claims: Christoffel symbols are the components of the Levi-Civita connection in a coordinate basis; they are determined entirely by the metric tensor and its first derivatives: Γᵏᵢⱼ = ½ gᵏˡ (∂ᵢ gⱡˡ + ∂ⱼ gᵢˡ − ∂ˡ gᵢⱼ).

On a flat surface in Cartesian coordinates all Christoffel symbols vanish, but on the same flat surface in polar coordinates they are nonzero — curvature is not the same as nonzero Christoffel symbols.
The covariant derivative ∇ᵢ Vʲ = ∂ᵢ Vʲ + Γʲᵢₖ Vᵏ corrects the ordinary derivative by subtracting the change in the basis vectors, giving a geometrically meaningful derivative on curved spaces.

Geodesic equations ẍᵏ + Γᵏᵢⱼ ẋⁱ ẋʲ = 0 are second-order ODEs whose solutions are the 'straightest possible' curves on the surface; Christoffel symbols act as the 'force' bending the coordinate trajectory.
Symmetry Γᵏᵢⱼ = Γᵏⱼᵢ (torsion-free) is a property of the Levi-Civita connection, not of arbitrary connections.

curvature tensor (Riemann) as the commutator of covariant derivatives

title: Theorien des Bewusstseins (Theories of Consciousness)
category_reason: It is a German interactive summary of Seth & Bayne (2022, Nature Reviews Neuroscience) comparing four scientific theories of consciousness; it is a philosophy-of-mind/neuroscience piece where AI is only a side-application.
thesis: A German interactive summary of Seth & Bayne (2022, Nature Reviews Neuroscience) comparing the four leading scientific theories of consciousness — Higher-Order Theories (HOT), Global Workspace Theory (GWT), Integrated Information Theory (IIT), and Predictive Processing / Re-Entry — across their core mechanisms, neural loci, and open problems, organized around Chalmers' 'hard problem'.
key_claims: The organizing question is Chalmers' hard problem: why is there subjective experience at all ('what it is like'), distinct from the 'easy' functional/behavioral problems; some theories (IIT, HOT) address it directly and some (GWT) deliberately bypass it.

HOT: a mental state becomes conscious when the brain represents it 'about itself' via a higher-order / meta-representation; located in the prefrontal cortex; explains mainly why some *contents* are conscious.

GWT: consciousness arises when information is 'ignited' and broadcast in a global (fronto-parietal) workspace — the 'bulletin board' of specialized modules; explains function and global states but not phenomenal quality.

IIT: consciousness IS the system's irreducible integrated information (Phi); derived from axioms about experience -> postulates -> identification; located in the posterior 'hot zone'; radical prediction that any system with Phi > 0 (even non-biological, e.g. photodiodes) is (something) conscious; Phi is practically uncomputable.

Predictive Processing / Re-Entry: perception is the brain's top-down 'best guess' and conscious content is that top-down prediction; Lamme's re-entry theory holds that local recurrent (posterior) processing suffices for consciousness while frontal regions are only needed for *report*.
The central localization debate is frontal (HOT/GWT) vs posterior (IIT/Re-Entry); 'No-Report' studies show frontal activity drops when no verbal report is needed, hinting it may serve only reporting.

The timing debate (early 120-200 ms supporting IIT/Re-Entry vs late 250-400 ms P3b supporting HOT/GWT) and the measurement problem (self-report circularity; the Perturbational Complexity Index as a non-report marker) are left open, with 'adversarial collaborations' (IIT vs GWT) proposed as a way forward.

internal_tensions: It is a neutral overview of a deeply contested field: frontal vs posterior localization, early vs late timing, and the hard-problem stance are all genuinely unresolved, and the tables' tick/mostly-not ratings encode one (reasonable but debatable) reading.

IIT's most distinctive claim — that non-biological systems and even photodiodes can be conscious — is flagged as 'contraintuitive' rather than resolved, and its Phi is 'practically uncomputable', so the theory's testability remains an open problem the piece admits.

The measurement problem (validating a consciousness marker without circular self-report) is left open; the piece presents the PCI as clinically useful but notes the fundamental validation gap, and its treatment of AI is only a side-application, not the focus.

title: Donaldsons Theorem — Interaktive Reise
category_reason: Main subject is Donaldson's theorem in 4-manifold differential topology and gauge theory — pure mathematics with no AI/ML connection.
thesis: Donaldson's theorem (1983) shows that if a smooth, closed, oriented 4-manifold has a definite intersection form, that form must be diagonalizable over the integers — a result so strong that it implies the existence of topological 4-manifolds that cannot be smoothed, proving that dimension 4 is fundamentally different from all other dimensions.
key_claims: The intersection form Q of a 4-manifold records the signed intersection numbers of all pairs of 2-cycles; it is a symmetric integer matrix.
If Q is definite (all eigenvalues same sign), Donaldson's theorem forces Q to be diagonalizable over ℤ, i.e., equivalent to ±I.
The proof uses Yang–Mills gauge theory: ASD (anti-self-dual) connections on an SU(2) bundle over the manifold form a moduli space whose topology constrains Q.
The E₈ lattice is a definite, unimodular intersection form that is not diagonalizable — so Freedman's topological 4-manifold with E₈ form cannot carry a smooth structure.
The cobordism argument: compactify the moduli space by gluing in copies of ℂP² at singularities and X at infinity; the signature invariant then forces n(Q) = rank(Q), hence diagonalizability.

thesis: Der Phasenraum eines dynamischen Systems ist in Einzugsgebiete (Basins of Attraction) zerlegt — Regionen, deren Trajektorien zum selben Attraktor konvergieren; die Grenzen (Separatrices) zwischen den Becken sind die 'Entscheidungsgrenzen', für multistabile/nichtlineare Systeme oft fraktal. Die interaktive Visualisierung (u.a. nach Datseris & Wagemakers 2021) zeigt die Becken einer Systemfamilie und wie Parameteränderungen verschieben, welchen Attraktor das System 'wählt'.
key_claims: Ein dynamisches System besitzt Attraktoren (Fixpunkte, Grenzzyklen, seltsame Attraktoren); jeder Attraktor hat ein Einzugsgebiet — die Menge aller Anfangszustände, die darauf zustreben.
Die Einzugsgebiete kacheln den Phasenraum; ihre Grenzen (Separatrices) sind die 'Entscheidungsgrenzen' zwischen Attraktoren.
Für nichtlineare/multistabile Systeme können die Becken fraktal sein und extrem parameter-empfindlich (chaotische Grenzen).
Die Becken-Struktur erklärt Bistabilität und Hysterese: Welcher Zustand sich einstellt, hängt vom Startpunkt (und von der Geschichte) ab.
Datseris & Wagemakers (2021) liefern eine Methode zur Schätzung/Visualisierung von Einzugsgebieten (z.B. durch Trajektorien-Integration und 'attractor-landscape'-Darstellung).
Parameteränderungen verformen die Becken — ein Attraktor kann schrumpfen, verschwinden oder sich spalten (Bifurkation).
visualizations: Plotly 2D: Becken-Diagramm (nach Attraktor gefärbt), animierte Trajektorien
Parameter-Sweep (Becken verformen sich live)
Separatrix / fraktale Grenz-Darstellung
Bistabilitäts-Demo (zwei stabile Zustände, Entscheidung durch Startpunkt)
internal_tensions: Beckengrenzen sind bei chaotischen Systemen fraktal; die diskrete Gitterauflösung der Visualisierung erfasst nur endlich viel Fraktal-Struktur.
'Welcher Attraktor' ist parameter-abhängig — ein einzelnes Becken-Bild ist ein Snapshot, nicht die volle Bifurkationsgeschichte.
Die Datseris-&-Wagemakers-Methode wird als Werkzeug herangezogen, aber ihre Genauigkeits-/Konvergenz-Eigenschaften werden nicht quantitativ behandelt.

title: Ehresmann Connection – Interactive Visual Explainer
category_reason: A pure differential-geometry exposition of Ehresmann connections on fibre bundles: vertical subspaces, horizontal distributions, parallel transport, and curvature/holonomy. No AI/ML content.
thesis: An interactive English-language visual guide to Ehresmann connections on fibre bundles: the user explores (1) what a fibre bundle is (total space E, base M, fibre F), (2) the vertical subspace (canonical, ker dπ), (3) choosing a horizontal distribution (the connection — not canonical), (4) parallel transport along curves (depends on the connection), and (5) curvature as the failure of the horizontal distribution to be integrable (holonomy after a closed loop).
key_claims: A fibre bundle π: E → M is a total space E that locally looks like M × F; the projection π maps each point in E to its base point in M.
At any point p ∈ E, the vertical subspace V_pE = ker(dπ_p) consists of tangent vectors that point along the fibre; this subspace is canonical (requires no extra choice).
An Ehresmann connection is a smooth choice of a horizontal subspace H_pE at every point such that T_pE = V_pE ⊕ H_pE; this choice is NOT canonical — there are many possible connections.

Once a connection is chosen, parallel transport along a curve in the base is defined by always moving in the horizontal direction (the unique lift of the base velocity into H_pE); different connections yield different transport results.

The curvature of a connection measures whether the horizontal distribution is integrable: if curvature is zero, parallel transport around any closed loop is trivial; if nonzero, you get holonomy (a net shift in the fibre after a round trip).
The connection angle slider demonstrates that the horizontal distribution is a choice: rotating the angle changes the connection, which changes the parallel transport result and the holonomy.
methods_math: fibre bundles: total space, base, fibre, projection
tangent space decomposition T_pE = V_pE ⊕ H_pE
parallel transport along curves via horizontal lift
curvature as integrability failure of the horizontal distribution
holonomy: fibre shift after parallel transport around a closed loop
visualizations: Fibre bundle explorer: drag a red point along the base manifold M; the fibre F above it is shown, with a blue dot in the total space E
Vertical subspace: move a point up and down the fibre to see the vertical tangent vector; the full tangent space T_pE is shown with the vertical component highlighted
Horizontal choice: an angle slider rotates the horizontal subspace H_pE relative to the vertical; 'Other possible horizontals' are shown as faded lines
Parallel transport: click 'Transport!' to watch a point in the fibre being carried along a base curve; change the connection angle to see different transport results
Curvature / holonomy: a curvature slider κ; 'Go Around Loop!' button; the holonomy (fibre shift after a closed loop) is displayed; κ = 0 gives trivial transport, κ > 0 gives a visible shift
internal_tensions: The file is a visual explainer, not a rigorous treatment: the mathematical definitions (fibre bundle, connection, curvature) are stated but not derived, and the relationship to the Levi-Civita connection (the canonical connection on the tangent bundle of a Riemannian manifold) is not discussed.

The 2D visualizations are necessarily reductive: real fibre bundles (e.g., principal bundles in gauge theory) have much richer structure, and the 'connection angle' is a 2D simplification that does not capture the full generality of connection 1-forms.

The holonomy demonstration is limited to a single closed loop on a 1D base; the full holonomy group (a subgroup of the structure group) and its relationship to the curvature via the Ambrose-Singer theorem are not discussed.

The file does not connect the Ehresmann connection to its physical applications (gauge theory, general relativity, Yang-Mills theory), where it is the central mathematical object; the connection is presented as a purely geometric concept.

title: Eigenvectors — See the Unseen Axes of Transformation
category_reason: Lineare Algebra (Eigenvektoren/Eigenwerte, Power Iteration) als reines Mathematik-Intuition mit generischen Anwendungen (PageRank, Schwingungsmoden, PCA, Quantenmechanik, Eigenfaces); kein explizites KI-/ML-Fokus im Framing.
thesis: Ein Eigenvektor v einer Matrix A ist ein nicht-nullicher Vektor, der unter A nicht die Richtung ändert, nur skaliert wird (Av=λv, λ Eigenwert); die Eigenvektoren sind die 'natürlichen Achsen' der Transformation, und wiederholte Anwendung (Power Iteration) richtet jeden Vektor entlang des dominierenden Eigenvektors aus – die Grundlage für PageRank, Schwingungsmoden, PCA und Stabilitätsanalyse.
key_claims: Ein Eigenvektor v von A erfüllt Av=λv: die Transformation skaliert v nur, dreht es nicht (es bleibt auf seiner Linie).
Die Eigenwerte sind die Lösungen der charakteristischen Gleichung det(A−λI)=0; für 2×2: λ²−(a+d)λ+(ad−bc)=0.
Ein reiner 2D-Drehung hat keine reellen Eigenvektoren (jede Richtung wird gedreht) – die Eigenwerte sind dann komplex.
Power Iteration: wiederholtes Multiplizieren eines Zufallsvektors mit A richtet ihn entlang des dominierenden Eigenvektors (größtes |λ|) aus.
Anwendung PageRank: die Wichtigkeit einer Webseite ist der dominierende Eigenvektor der Link-Matrix des Webs.
Anwendung Schwingungsmoden: die Moden einer Brücke/Saite/Gebäudes sind Eigenvektoren der Steifigkeitsmatrix; der Eigenwert gibt die Frequenz.
Anwendung PCA: die Hauptkomponenten sind Eigenvektoren der Kovarianzmatrix der Daten – die Richtungen maximaler Varianz.
Anwendung Stabilitätsanalyse: ein System ist stabil, wenn alle Eigenwerte Betrag <1 haben; es oszilliert/explodiert je nach Lage der Eigenwerte.
Quiz: Skalierung (3,2) → Eigenvektoren sind die Achsen; λ₁=5, λ₂=0.1 nach 100 Anwendungen → Ausrichtung an v₁ und enormes Wachstum; 90°-Drehung → keine reellen Eigenvektoren.

internal_tensions: Das Framing ist reine lineare Algebra; die ML-Adjazenzen (PCA, Eigenfaces, Stabilität des Trainings) werden als 'Anwendungen' gelistet, aber nicht vertieft – die Brücke zu KI fehlt.
Die Power-Iteration wird 2D-visuell gezeigt; der Konvergenz-Beweis (Spektral-Lücke |λ₁|>|λ₂|) wird nicht erklärt.
Die Quiz-Antworten sind binär richtig/falsch – der lerntheoretische Wert ist begrenzt, und es werden keine Fälle mit multiplen/doppeln Eigenwerten (nicht-diagonalisierbar) behandelt.

thesis: Der Körper als System: alles Essen besteht aus Kohlenhydraten/Fetten/Protein; die Energiebilanz (Aufnahme − Verbrauch) entscheidet über Zunahme/Abnahme (~7700 kcal = 1 kg Fett), und Makro-Verteilung, Blutzucker-Spikes und Fettart haben konkrete gesundheitliche Konsequenzen.
key_claims: Alles Essen besteht aus drei Bausteinen: Kohlenhydrate (→ Zucker → Energie/Fett), Fette (→ Energie/Speicher/Zellbau), Protein (→ Muskeln/Reparatur); Überschuss wird als Fett gespeichert.
Energiebilanz: z.B. 2400 kcal Aufnahme − 2100 kcal Verbrauch = +300 kcal/Tag → Zunahme; ~7700 kcal Überschuss = 1 kg Fett.
Ideal für Abnehmen + stabilen Blutzucker: ~40 % Kohlenhydrate, ~30 % Fett, ~30 % Protein; zu viele (schnelle) Kohlenhydrate = Blutzucker-Spikes = Schwitzen/Heißhunger/Fetteinlagerung.

title: Exotic Spheres - Visual Explorer
category_reason: Reine Mathematik: exotische Sphären (topologisch Sphäre, aber glatt unterschiedlich); Milnors Entdeckung (28 in Dimension 7), Smooth Poincaré in Dimension 4 (offen). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Eine exotische Sphäre ist topologisch eine gewöhnliche Sphäre (keine Löcher, gleiche Konnektivität), aber glatt 'verdreht' – eine glatte Struktur, die sich durch keine glatte Deformation auf die Standard-Sphäre bringen lässt; Milnor (1956) zeigte, dass es in Dimension 7 genau 28 solche glatten Strukturen gibt, und in Dimension 4 bleibt die Existenz offener exotischer Sphären eines der großen ungelösten Probleme.
key_claims: Eine Sphäre ist jede Form, die sich stetig (strecken, stauchen, beugen – ohne Reißen/Verkleben) in einen runden Ball deformieren lässt; Topologie fragt nur nach Löchern.
Eine glatte Struktur ist ein 'Atlas' von Koordinatenkarten, die sich glatt überlappen; für die Standard-Sphäre sind die Übergangsabbildungen glatt.
Eine exotische Sphäre hat denselben Topologie-Typ, aber ihre glatte Struktur ist 'verdreht' – die Verdrehung ist in der glatten Struktur 'eingebrennt' und lässt sich nicht glatt entfernen.
Milnor (1956): in Dimension 7 gibt es genau 28 glatte Strukturen auf der Sphäre (1 Standard + 27 exotisch).
Dimension 4 ist der Mysterien-Fall: ob exotische 4-Sphären existieren, ist offen (Smooth Poincaré-Vermutung in Dimension 4).

Die Verklebungs-Analogie: klebe zwei Halbkugeln entlang ihres Äquators; eine verdrehte Verklebung (eine Halbkugel vor dem Verkleben gedreht) ergibt topologisch eine Sphäre, aber eine glatt unterschiedliche.
Die Anzahl explodiert: Dimension 11 hat 992, Dimension 15 hat 16.256, Dimension 31 hat ~16,9 Millionen exotische Sphären.
visualizations: Canvas: topologische Sphäre (rund/gequetscht/klumpig/stachelig, alle homöomorph)
Canvas: Atlas / glatte Struktur (Standard vs. exotische Karten, Überlappungen)
Canvas: die Verdrehung (Flow-Lines am Äquator, τ-Parameter)
Canvas: Dimensions-Explorer (Sphären pro Dimension, Fragezeichen für Dim 4)
Canvas: Verklebungs-Analogie (4 Schritte: zwei Hälften → Standard → exotisch → Vergleich)
Canvas: interaktive Morphing-Explorer (Drag-Rotation, τ-Parameter, 3 Modi)
internal_tensions: Die 'Verdrehung' wird als Flow-Lines am Äquator visualisiert – das ist eine starke Vereinfachung, die die echte glatte Struktur (Parallelisierungsproblem) nicht zeigt.
Die Zählung (28 in Dim 7, 992 in Dim 11, …) wird behauptet, aber der Nachweis (via Kervaire-Milnor, exakte Folgen) fehlt komplett.
Die Smooth Poincaré-Vermutung in Dimension 4 wird als 'offen' genannt – korrekt, aber die Nuance (sie ist äquivalent zur 4D-Smooth-Poincaré, einander ungelöst) wird nur angerissen.

title: Faserbündel & Fibrationen - Eine interaktive Reise
category_reason: Pure differential geometry / algebraic topology (fiber bundles, fibrations, homotopy); no AI content
thesis: German interactive tour of fiber bundles and fibrations following Sorensen's 'An Introduction to Fiber Bundles and Fibrations': local vs global structure, transition functions and the cocycle condition, vector bundles, the Hopf fibration S1->S3->S2, the homotopy lifting property, the vertical tangent bundle ker Df, and the long exact sequence yielding pi_1(S1)=Z and pi_i(S2) isomorphic to pi_i(S3) for i>2.
key_claims: Local != global: a space can be locally a product (trivial) yet globally twisted (Mobius); the twist is invisible in any single chart
A fiber bundle is a space E -> B where each fiber pi^-1(b) looks like F; transition functions g_ab : U_a cap U_b -> Aut(F) must satisfy the cocycle condition g_ab * g_bc * g_ca = I
Vector bundles (fiber = R^k) are the special case; the Mobius bundle is non-trivial because every section must have a zero (intermediate value theorem)
The Hopf fibration S1 -> S3 -> S2 is the canonical non-trivial bundle; its fibers are linked circles with integer Hopf invariant
A fibration generalizes a bundle by replacing 'local triviality' with the homotopy lifting property (HLP); every continuous map can be replaced by a homotopy-equivalent fibration
The vertical tangent bundle T_f := ker Df consists of directions tangent to the fibers - movement that does not change the base point
The long exact sequence in homotopy for a fibration F -> E -> B connects pi_n(F), pi_n(E), pi_n(B) in a balance equation (exactness: im = ker)
Applying the long exact sequence: pi_1(S1) = Z (via universal cover R -> S1), and pi_i(S2) isomorphic to pi_i(S3) for all i > 2 (via Hopf fibration), so pi_3(S2) = Z - counterintuitively non-zero

title: Feedback Loops — Visual Mental Model
category_reason: A general systems-thinking explainer about positive (reinforcing) and negative (balancing) feedback loops, with examples from finance, biology, ecology, and social systems. No AI/ML content.
thesis: An interactive English-language mental model for feedback loops: positive (reinforcing) loops amplify small changes into exponential growth or collapse, negative (balancing) loops self-correct toward a target (homeostasis), and real systems combine both to produce the S-curve (logistic growth with carrying capacity). Each loop type is illustrated with a live simulation and six real-world examples.
key_claims: Positive (reinforcing) feedback: the output amplifies the input; small changes snowball into massive effects. This is the engine behind exponential growth (compound interest, viral spread) and exponential collapse (anxiety spirals, market crashes).

Positive feedback loops are inherently unstable — they always accelerate toward explosion or collapse; nothing in nature grows forever. When you spot a positive loop, always ask: 'What will eventually stop this?'

Negative (balancing) feedback: the system self-corrects toward a target; deviations are counteracted. This is the engine behind stability, homeostasis, and regulation (thermostats, blood sugar, supply & demand).
Negative feedback loops create stability but can also create stagnation: every system that 'resists change' is running a balancing loop. To change, you must disrupt the loop or change the target.
Real systems have both loops running simultaneously: a positive loop drives growth, but a negative loop enforces a carrying capacity, producing the S-curve (logistic growth).

The S-curve is ubiquitous: population growth, technology adoption, product lifecycles, and organizational growth all follow the same pattern of initial exponential growth, slowing as resources constrain, and eventual saturation.
methods_math: positive feedback: x_{n+1} = x_n · (1 + r) (exponential growth)
negative feedback: error-driven correction toward a setpoint (first-order system)
combined loops: logistic growth dx/dt = r·x·(1 - x/K)
carrying capacity K as the saturation level
homeostasis: negative feedback maintaining a variable within a range
S-curve (sigmoid) as the universal growth pattern
visualizations: Positive feedback simulation: canvas showing exponential growth with adjustable feedback strength (growth rate) and starting value; 'Run' and 'Reset' buttons
Negative feedback simulation: canvas showing error-driven correction toward a target with adjustable correction strength and disturbance size
Combined S-curve simulation: canvas showing logistic growth where a positive loop drives growth and a negative loop enforces carrying capacity
Six real-world examples per loop type: compound interest, viral spread, anxiety spirals (positive); thermostat, blood sugar, supply & demand (negative); etc.
Key insight callouts: 'What will eventually stop this?' (positive), 'To change, disrupt the loop or change the target' (negative)
internal_tensions: The file presents feedback loops as a universal mental model, but the simulations are 1D and linear; real feedback systems are often multi-variable, nonlinear, and delayed, which can produce oscillations, chaos, or other behaviors not captured by the simple models.

The 'S-curve is everywhere' claim is strong but potentially overgeneralized: many real-world growth processes follow power laws, stretched exponentials, or multiple successive S-curves (technological paradigm shifts) rather than a single logistic curve.

The file does not discuss the role of time delays in feedback loops, which are often the source of oscillation and instability in real systems (e.g., the cobweb model in economics, predator-prey cycles in ecology).
The six examples per loop type are illustrative but not quantitatively grounded; the file does not provide parameters or data, so the 'mental model' is qualitative rather than predictive.

title: Interactive Fiber Bundles Explorer
category_reason: Reine Differentialtopologie: Faserbündel interaktiv erkunden (triviales Zylinder-Bündel, Möbius-Band, Tangentialbündel von S¹, Hopf-Faserung, Custom-Builder mit Twist/Faser-Steuerung). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Ein Faserbündel ist ein topologischer Raum (Totalraum E), der lokal wie ein Produkt (Basis B × Faser F) aussieht, aber global 'verdreht' sein kann; die klassischen Beispiele (triviales Zylinder-Bündel, verdrehtes Möbius-Band, Tangentialbündel des Kreises, Hopf-Faserung S³→S²) zeigen, wie lokale Trivialität globale Struktur verbergen kann, und ein interaktiver Builder lässt Bündel durch Wahl von Basis, Faser und Verdrehung konstruieren.
key_claims: Ein Faserbündel π: E → B hat einen Totalraum E, eine Basis B und eine Faser F, mit lokalen Trivialisierungen (E sieht über offenen Teilmengen U ⊂ B aus wie U × F).
Das triviale Bündel ist einfach ein Produkt B × F (z.B. ein Zylinder); die Faser zu 'verdrillen', während man die Basis entlang geht, ergibt nicht-triviale Bündel (z.B. das Möbius-Band).
Das Tangentialbündel des Kreises S¹ ist trivial (S¹ × ℝ) — man kann ein Vektorfeld rundherum 'kämmen' ohne Singularität (im Gegensatz zu S²).
Die Hopf-Faserung S³ → S² hat Kreise als Fasern — eine 3-Sphäre ist ein Bündel von Kreisen über einer 2-Sphäre.
Die Verdrehung (Monodromie / Übergangsabbildungen) ist es, was Bündel unterscheidet; die 'Twist-Zahl' im Builder steuert die globale Struktur.
Lokale Trivialität + nicht-triviale globale Verklebung = der Kern des Faserbündel-Begriffs.

Canvas 3D: Möbius-Band (verdrehtes Bündel)

internal_tensions: Die Hopf-Faserung (S³→S²) ist in 3D schwer darzustellen (S³ ist 4-dim); die Projektion ist eine Vereinfachung.
Die 'Twist-Zahl' im Builder erfasst die einfachste (abelsche) Verdrehung; allgemeine Bündel haben nicht-abelsche Übergangsabbildungen, die hier nicht vollständig erfasst werden.
Die 3D-Visualisierung von 4-dim Totalräumen (S³) ist eine Projektion mit Informationsverlust — die echte Faserung bleibt abstrakt.

title: Fiber Bundles Lab
category_reason: English interactive lab on fiber bundles: visualizing principal bundles, associated bundles, connections (gauge fields), and curvature, with both Plotly 3D cross-sections and three.js bundle renderings. Pure differential geometry / gauge theory with no AI content.
thesis: An interactive English-language lab that builds intuition for fiber bundles from the ground up: what a total space, base, and fiber are, how a connection (gauge field) lets you compare fibers at different base points (parallel transport), and how curvature measures the failure of parallel transport to be path-independent — with 3D renderings of common examples (trivial bundle, Möbius strip, SU(2) bundle).
key_claims: A fiber bundle is a surjection π: E -> B such that every point in B has a neighborhood whose preimage looks like U × F (local triviality); the 'fiber' F is the space you get by looking straight down at a base point.

A connection on a principal G-bundle is a choice of 'horizontal direction' at each point of E, equivalent to a Lie-algebra-valued 1-form ω satisfying equivariance and reproducing the fundamental vertical vectors; in physics this is the gauge potential A.
Parallel transport along a path γ in the base lifts γ to a horizontal path in E; the endpoint depends on the path if and only if the curvature F = dω + ½[ω,ω] is nonzero.

Holonomy: transporting a vector around a closed loop in the base and comparing it to the original gives an element of the structure group G; the collection of all holonomies is the holonomy group, which (by Ambrose-Singer) is generated by curvature.

The trivial bundle B × F has zero curvature and a global section; the Möbius strip is the simplest nontrivial line bundle over S¹ with structure group Z/2; the Hopf fibration S³ -> S² with fiber S¹ is the prototype for SU(2) gauge theory.
methods_math: fiber bundle definition: surjection + local triviality
principal G-bundle and structure group action
associated bundles via quotient E ×_G F
visualizations: three.js rendering of a 3D fiber bundle: base as a colored surface, fibers as vertical lines/tubes, with a 'gauge' slider that twists the fibers to show nontriviality
Plotly 3D cross-section: a principal bundle over a 2D base shown as a 3D manifold with the group action visualized as rotations of the fiber

parallel transport animation: a vector in the fiber is transported around a small loop in the base; the holonomy angle is displayed as a function of loop area (showing curvature = area × field strength)
Möbius strip vs. cylinder comparison: two side-by-side 3D renderings with a vector being transported around the core circle, showing the sign flip for the Möbius strip
internal_tensions: The lab presents gauge theory as 'just geometry', but the physical interpretation (local symmetry as a redundancy in description) is only lightly touched; the mathematical formalism and the physical motivation are not fully reconciled.

title: Frege's Grundlagen der Arithmetik — Interactive Explorer
category_reason: An English-language interactive explorer for Gottlob Frege's 1884 'Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik': anti-psychologism, the concept/object distinction, numbers as properties of concepts, extensions, Hume's Principle (equinumerosity), the definitions of 0, 1, 2, ..., and the Context Principle. Philosophy of mathematics / logic, no AI/ML.
thesis: An interactive English-language explorer for the 7 key ideas in Frege's 'Grundlagen der Arithmetik' (1884): (1) anti-psychologism (numbers are not mental images), (2) the concept/object distinction, (3) numbers attach to concepts, not objects, (4) extensions of concepts, (5) Hume's Principle (equinumerosity), (6) the logical definitions of 0, 1, 2, ..., and (7) the Context Principle. Each idea has an interactive visualization (sliders, toggles, click-to-explore) that makes the abstract concept concrete.
key_claims: Anti-psychologism: numbers are objective, mind-independent entities, not mental images or ideas in our heads. If numbers were mental images, then 'your 3' and 'my 3' would be different, and arithmetic would collapse into subjective psychology. The interactive: a slider for 'how many people are thinking of 5' — the number 5 remains the same regardless.

Concept/object distinction: a concept is a predicate (a function from objects to truth-values); an object is something that falls under a concept. The concept 'is even' maps 2 -> TRUE, 3 -> FALSE. The interactive: select a concept (even, prime, > N, perfect square) and watch which objects fall under it.

Numbers attach to concepts, not objects: 'there are 3 apples' means the concept 'apple on the table' has 3 objects falling under it, not that the apples have the property '3'. The same physical pile can be '1 deck' or '52 cards' depending on the concept applied. The interactive: a slider for pairs of shoes, with toggles for 'count pairs' / 'count individual shoes' / 'count soles' — the count changes while the physical situation stays the same.

Extensions: the extension of a concept F is the set of all objects falling under F. Two concepts have the same number iff their extensions are equinumerous (there exists a bijection between them). The interactive: two sliders for the sizes of extensions of F and G; when they match, a bijection is shown.

Hume's Principle: #F = #G iff F and G are equinumerous. This is the key criterion for when two concepts share a number — without needing to say what numbers are first. The interactive: two groups of apples and stars; when they match, a 1-to-1 correspondence (bijection) is shown.

Definitions of 0, 1, 2, ...: 0 = the number belonging to the concept 'is not identical with itself' (empty extension); 1 = the number belonging to 'is identical with 0'; 2 = the number belonging to 'is identical with 0 or 1'; etc. Each number is defined from the previous ones. The interactive: a slider that builds up the natural numbers one by one, showing the defining concept and extension at each step.

Context Principle: never ask for the meaning of a word in isolation, but only in the context of a sentence. The meaning of '3' is determined by the truth-values of all sentences in which it appears ('3 = 3', '3 + 1 = 4', '3 is prime', '3 > 2', etc.), not by pointing at a mental image or a physical heap. The interactive: select a number n, and see the list of sentences containing n with their truth-values.

internal_tensions: The file is a pedagogical explorer, not a philosophical argument; the 7 ideas are presented as a linear progression, but in the 'Grundlagen' they are interdependent and the order is not strictly linear (e.g., the Context Principle is stated in the introduction and used throughout).

The Russell paradox (which destroyed Frege's logicist program in 1902) is mentioned in the overview but not developed; the file presents Frege's system as if it were successful, without discussing the paradox or its consequences.

The 'numbers as logical objects' claim is the most controversial; the file presents it as Frege's view but does not discuss the alternative (e.g., structuralism, fictionalism, the 'no unique answer' problem for the interpretation of Frege's definitions).

The file is in English and uses Frege's German terms in translation; some terms (e.g., 'Begriff' = concept, 'Gegenstand' = object, 'Umfang' = extension) are consistently translated, but the 'Grundlagen' section numbers (§46, §63, §74) are cited without the German text, which may be confusing for readers who want to check the original.

title: The Science of FUN
category_reason: Neurowissenschaft: die Wissenschaft von Spass/Freude (Belohnungssystem, Dopamin, Flow, Spiel, Neugier). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Spass/Freude ist ein neurobiologischer Prozess: Das Belohnungssystem des Gehirns (Dopamin als 'wanting'/Antizipation, opioide/Endocannabinoide als 'liking'/momentane Freude) erzeugt Freude; 'Fun' entsteht, wenn eine Aktivität diese Belohnungskreise mit optimaler Herausforderung (Flow — weder zu leicht noch zu schwer), Neugier, Überraschung und Kompetenz aktiviert. Die interaktiven Diagramme zerlegen den Belohnungslauf in seine Komponenten.
key_claims: Freude hat zwei Komponenten: die momentane hedonische Freude ('liking') und die antizipierende Freude ('wanting') auf eine belohnende Zukunft.
Dopamin ist primär das 'wanting'/Belohnungs-Prädiktions-Signal (Verlangen, Antizipation), nicht die Freude selbst — die 'liking'-Empfindung trägt mehr Opioide/Endocannabinoide.
Flow (Csikszentmihalyi): Spass braucht optimale Herausforderung — die Schwierigkeit muss zur Fähigkeit passen (zu leicht = Langeweile, zu schwer = Angst).
Neugier, Überraschung und Spiel sind zentrale Treiber von Spass: ungelöste Information ('Information-Gap') und das 'Was-wäre-wenn' halten den Belohnungskreis aktiv.
Meisterhaftigkeit/Kompetenz (mastery) und die Möglichkeit zu spielen (ohne externe Belohnung) verstärken die Freude — intrinsische Motivation.
Der Belohnungslauf ist ein Feedback-Zyklus: Antizipation → Handlung → Belohnung → Lernen → neue Antizipation.

internal_tensions: Die Unterscheidung 'Dopamin = wanting, nicht liking' ist eine starke Vereinfachung umstrittener Neurowissenschaft (Berridge & Robinson) und wird hier als Konsens präsentiert.
'Fun' ist ein Volksbegriff; seine Zerlegung in Belohnungskreise ist reduktiv und übersieht kulturelle/soziale Dimensionen von Spass.
Die Flow-Kurve ist eine glatte, schematische Darstellung — reale Motivation ist rauschiger und von Kontext abhängig.

title: Kohärente Welt — Garben, Keime, Situs
category_reason: It is a German slide-deck (arrow-key presentation) that builds sheaf/germ/situs and infinity-coherence theory from the ground up (point -> neighborhood -> measurement -> stalk -> germ -> gluing -> situs -> limits); it is pure math (sheaf and infinity-category theory) with no ML/neural-net focus.
thesis: A German slide-deck, 'Kohärente Welt' (a coherent world), that reconstructs the sheaf-theoretic worldview step by step: from a single point, to a neighborhood (without distance), to a measurement (thermometer -> number), to a stalk (many measurements at one point), to germs (behaviour in arbitrarily small neighbourhoods), to compatibility/incompatibility on overlaps (where incompatibility is glossed as measurement error, wrong model, lie, or 'hallucination'), to the presheaf -> sheaf gluing condition, to an infinity-sheaf / infinity-coherence upgrade, and finally to situs and limits.
key_claims: The whole sheaf-theoretic vocabulary can be built up from a single point: a point, then a neighbourhood (a notion of 'near' without any metric/distance), then a measurement (a thermometer that turns a point into a number).

Many measurements at the same point (temperature, colour, tone, humidity, pressure, ...) bundle into a stalk (Halm); a germ (Keim) is the behaviour of a local section in arbitrarily small neighbourhoods of a point.

On overlapping neighbourhoods, two local sections are compatible iff their restrictions agree on the overlap (s_1|_{U intersect V} = s_2|_{U intersect V}); when they disagree (s_1| != s_2|) that signals a measurement error, a wrong model, a different object, a lie, or a 'hallucination'.
The presheaf -> sheaf step is the gluing condition: compatible local sections glue to a single global section; a sheaf is exactly the data where local information coheres into global information.

The 'Blitz und Donner' (lightning and thunder) slide exposes the subtlety: two stalks with the same origin that are NOT equal on the time axis; they are reconciled by an equalizer (f(x) = g(y), e.g. t_Ton = t_Blitz + d/v_Schall), so the stalks are 'homotopic' (connected by a reversible transformation).

The infinity-sheaf / infinity-coherence (infinite-Koherenz) step generalizes the classical sheaf gluing to higher coherences, and the deck closes by moving to situs and to limits — the abstract, category-theoretic form of 'a coherent world'.
methods_math: points, neighbourhoods and a notion of 'near' without a metric
measurements / sections and the stalk (Halm) at a point
germs (Keime) as equivalence classes of sections in arbitrarily small neighbourhoods
the compatibility condition on overlaps and the presheaf -> sheaf gluing (COM) condition
equalizers and reversible (homotopy-like) identifications of stalks
situs and limits (the categorical generalization of a coherent world)
visualizations: an arrow-key slide-deck (click/keyboard navigation) of ~14+ slides, each with one or more Plotly plots
Plotly slides building up the vocabulary: a point, a neighbourhood (without distance), a thermometer measurement (space + value), many measurements at one point (stalk)
Plotly slides for germs, multiple germs, overlapping neighbourhoods, the compatible (equal-on-overlap) case and the incompatible case
a presheaf -> sheaf gluing plot, a 'Blitz und Donner' (lightning/thunder) plot, and the equalizer (f(x)=g(y)) plot showing the homotopy/reversible-identification
a classic-vs-infinity-sheaf comparison and plots for the infinity-coherence concept, situs, and limits
a closing 'coherent-not-true' Plotly plot (coherence is not the same as truth)
internal_tensions: The load-bearing tension is coherence-vs-truth: compatible local data glues into a global object (coherence), but coherence is explicitly NOT truth — the deck carries a dedicated 'coherent but not true' slide to keep the two apart.

Incompatibility on overlaps is the flashpoint: the same mathematical condition (disagreement on the overlap) is glossed in many different ways (measurement error, wrong model, different object, lie, hallucination), which is a deliberate interpretive stretch from pure sheaf theory.

The leap from classical sheaves to infinity-sheaves / situs / limits is the big conceptual jump; the deck presents it as a natural upgrade, but it is the move from a set-valued gluing condition to higher-categorical coherence.

title: 🚂 Garbentheorie des vorbeifahrenden Zuges
category_reason: A pure sheaf-theory pedagogy piece using the metaphor of a passing train: germs, stalks, sections, presheaves, and the gluing axiom. No AI/ML content whatsoever.
thesis: An interactive German-language walkthrough of sheaf theory built around the concrete metaphor of watching a train pass by: from the germ (what you perceive at a single instant) through the stalk (all sensory modalities at that point), the section (the film over a time interval), the presheaf (all possible film clips), to the sheaf (the unique global event — the train — that local data glue together to form).
key_claims: A germ [s]_x is an equivalence class of sections that agree on some arbitrarily small neighborhood of x; formally, the stalk F_x is the direct limit over the directed system of open neighborhoods of x.

The stalk at a point decomposes as a direct sum of modality-specific stalks (visual ⊕ auditory ⊕ vibrational ⊕ pressure ⊕ temperature), modeling independent sensory channels as a product sheaf F = ∏ᵢ F⁽ⁱ⁾.
A section s ∈ F(U) over an open set U is a compatible assignment of local data; restriction morphisms ρ^U_V satisfy the functoriality condition ρ^V_W ∘ ρ^U_V = ρ^U_W.
A presheaf is a contravariant functor F: Op(X)^op → Ab (or Set, Mod_R); it collects local data but does not yet guarantee that local data from different sensors belong to the same global object.

The sheaf condition (gluing + local uniqueness) is what turns a presheaf into a sheaf: if local sections agree on all overlaps, they glue to a unique global section. This is expressed as the equalizer sequence F(U) → ∏ᵢ F(Uᵢ) ⇉ ∏_{i,j} F(Uᵢ ∩ Uⱼ).
The étale space (disjoint union of all stalks) π: Ét(F) → X provides the geometric picture: the stalk F_x is the fiber of π over x, and sections are continuous sections of this space.
methods_math: germs, stalks, direct limits over directed systems
sections, restriction morphisms, presheaves as contravariant functors
equalizer sequence for the sheaf condition
product sheaves for independent modality bundles
open covers, category Op(X) of open sets
visualizations: Interactive timeline: a train passes along the x-axis (time); click to select a point, see the germ; drag to select an interval U, see the section
Doppler sound: audio playback simulates the train's approaching/receding pitch shift, synced to the timeline
Stalk visualization: at the selected point, a vertical stack of sensory modality icons (light, sound, vibration, pressure, temperature) represents the stalk F_x
Presheaf collection: all possible time windows and their associated 'film clips' are shown as a growing library
Gluing demo: two sections (visual + auditory) over overlapping intervals; a 'Bereit' (Ready) button triggers the gluing when they agree on the overlap, producing the single global object 'DER Zug'
Canvas-based train animation with the observer's perspective changing as the train passes
internal_tensions: The train metaphor is vivid but potentially misleading: a real train event is temporally bounded and causally connected, whereas sheaf-theoretic gluing is a purely local-to-global principle that does not require causal structure.

The file treats the sensory modalities as a direct sum (independent channels), but in real perception the modalities are cross-calibrated (e.g., lip-reading helps hearing); the product-sheaf model does not capture this coupling.

The gluing axiom is presented as 'the magic' that produces the unique global train, but the file does not discuss what happens when the local data do NOT agree on overlaps (the presheaf fails to be a sheaf) — a case that is arguably more interesting in practice.

The mathematical notation (direct limits, equalizer sequences, étale spaces) is introduced without derivation; the file assumes the reader can follow the formalism or is satisfied with the metaphor as a heuristic.

title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems — Interactive Explorer
category_reason: Interactive explanation of Gödel's incompleteness theorems (logic / foundations of mathematics); no AI application.
thesis: Gödel's first theorem says any consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains true-but-unprovable statements (via a self-referential Gödel sentence G = 'I am not provable'); the second theorem says such a system cannot prove its own consistency — so you must sacrifice completeness or consistency, and consistency proofs always require a stronger system.
key_claims: First Incompleteness Theorem: any consistent system strong enough to express arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove; adding axioms does not remove this as long as it stays consistent.
Gödel numbering: every symbol/formula/proof gets a unique number via a prime-power product, letting the system reason about its own sentences arithmetically.
The Gödel sentence G = 'I am not provable in S': if G is provable → contradiction (a consistent system can't prove a falsehood); so G is not provable, hence G is true-but-unprovable.
Consistency vs completeness trade-off: you cannot have both in a sufficiently powerful system; a system proving 'everything' is trivially inconsistent.
Second Incompleteness Theorem: 'S is consistent' is equivalent to G, so it is also unprovable in S; proving consistency needs a strictly stronger system — 'turtles all the way down'.
An inconsistent system 'proves' almost anything (useless, proves contradictions).
methods_math: formal systems / axioms and proof rules
Gödel (arithmetization) numbering via prime powers / BigInt
visualizations: DOM: formal-system statement grid (provable / true-unprovable / independent) driven by axiom-strength, statement-count and consistency sliders; live Gödel-numbering of a typed formula (per-symbol prime-power chips + BigInt product); SVG self-reference loop that animates under the two assumptions of G; Canvas: consistency-vs-completeness trade-off plane with an 'IMPOSSIBLE (by Gödel)' region and a moving system dot; a button-driven 'attempt to prove own consistency' sequence ending in a shattering mirror box.
internal_tensions: The statement-grid 'provable/true-unprovable' split is a synthetic, seeded-rng simulation, not a real consistency/completeness computation — it conveys the flavor but not the actual arithmetized proof.
Framing the second theorem as 'turtles all the way down' leans into a popular (somewhat uncharitable) reading of foundational regress that formalists dispute.
The consistency-off slider implies inconsistency lets you prove 'almost anything', which is correct but glosses over the principle of explosion.

title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems — Interactive Explainer
category_reason: A pure math-logic explainer of Gödel's incompleteness theorems; AI is only mentioned in passing as a ripple effect.
thesis: An interactive tabbed explainer of Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems: Gödel numbering lets mathematics talk about itself, and a self-referential formula G ('G is not provable') is true yet unprovable — so no sufficiently strong, consistent, recursively-axiomatized system is complete, nor can it prove its own consistency.
key_claims: Gödel numbering encodes symbols/formulas/proofs as natural numbers via prime factorization, making 'provability' an arithmetic (recursive) property.
The formula R(q);q asserts its own unprovability — a liar-paradox made rigorous, true but unprovable inside the system.
First Incompleteness (Satz VI): every omega-consistent recursive class of formulas has undecidable formulas.
Second Incompleteness (Satz XI): a consistent system cannot prove its own consistency.
Theorem VII: every recursive relation is arithmetical; Theorem X: the first-order Entscheidungsproblem is undecidable.
This killed Hilbert's program and influenced Turing (halting), Church, Cohen (CH independent of ZFC); Penrose's 'mind transcends algorithms' is flagged as controversial.

interactive Gödel-number calculator (BigInt prime powers) + symbol grid

internal_tensions: Uses the original (stronger) omega-consistency statement of the 1st theorem; modern versions use mere consistency (Rosser).
The Penrose/mind claims are presented as a controversial ripple, not endorsed.

key_claims: Das System hat 9 Schritte (ethische Prinzipien), 8 Axiome und 14 bewiesene Theoreme — ein vollständiger, formalisierbarer Aufbau.

Garben-theoretische Konsistenz: Man legt eine Garbe über den Lebensraum; offene Mengen sind Kontexte/Domänen, Schnitte die Prinzipien in diesem Kontext, und das Verklebungstheorem (Gluing) besagt: lokal widerspruchsfreie Prinzipien kleben zu einem globalen, kohärenten Leben.
Formale Verifikation in Coq/abhängiger Typentheorie: Jedes Theorem ist ein Typ, jeder Beweis ein Programm; verifiziert heißt maschinell geprüft, nicht nur behauptet.
Verbindung zu anderen Axiomensystemen: Die Methode spiegelt, wie physikalische (Maxwell), logische (ZFC) und mathematische Axiome aufgebaut sind — Einheit durch Struktur, nicht durch Inhalt.
Jedes Prinzip ist lokal anwendbar; die Garben-Axiome (Lokalität + Verklebung) garantieren, dass keine lokalen Widersprüche global entstehen.

title: How to Live Well — A Formally Verified Ethical Logic
category_reason: Formal ethics / applied mathematics, not machine learning. It builds an axiomatic ethical system whose internal contradictions are resolved and whose global consistency is certified by a sheaf-theoretic gluing condition and machine-checked in Coq. No neural networks, training, or data/learning involved.
thesis: A complete, self-consistent ethics can be written down as an explicit axiomatic system in which every principle is bundled with its own failure modes and edge-case resolutions, conflicts are settled by an explicit priority ordering and contextual weighting, and global consistency is certified by the sheaf gluing condition (local sections must agree on overlaps) and machine-verified in Coq.
key_claims: The system consists of 10 principles, 12 axioms, 47 theorems, and 23 edge-case resolutions.
Ethical principles are modeled as sheaf sections over five 'open sets' (domains): Self, Other, Community, Temporal, Emergency.
Consistency is the sheaf gluing axiom: on overlaps (e.g. Self ∩ Other) the harm-assessment sections must agree — you cannot score your own harm as zero on Self and nonzero on Other.
Each axiom is also assigned a category-theoretic role (e.g. minimize-net-harm is the initial object / universal lower bound that every other principle factors through).
Conflicts between principles are deemed inevitable and are resolved by explicit priority ordering and contextual weighting rather than by retraction.
Twelve bedrock values are stated as chosen, not proved, and each carries its own vulnerability to critique.
Classic dilemmas are resolved explicitly (Trolley Problem, Ticking Time Bomb, Omission vs Commission, Aggregation, Moral Luck, Self-Sacrifice, Future Persons).
Principles are grounded in lived examples and counter-examples (Janusz Korczak, Harriet Tubman, Semmelweis, WWI tit-for-tat, Frederick Douglass, Unit 731, Theranos, Leopold II, climate denial).
Every proof is meant to be explicit and step-by-step, available in natural language, as philosophical argument, and machine-checkable in Coq.
methods_math: Sheaf theory: sections over open sets plus the gluing condition as a local-to-global consistency certificate.
Category theory: initial/limit objects and factorization to encode principle priority.
Priority ordering / contextual weighting as a conflict-resolution (weighting) rule.
visualizations: Data-driven single-page app: all content lives in a JS object (no static headings), defaulting to a 'steps' view.
Interactive principle/axiom navigation; each principle expands to definition, expansion, sheaf condition, category role, edge cases, and a Coq snippet.
Sheaf domain diagram: the five open sets (Self/Other/Community/Temporal/Emergency) with explicit overlap-gluing annotations.
internal_tensions: Claims machine-verifiable consistency while resting on twelve explicitly chosen (unproved) bedrock values — the axioms are stipulated, not derived.
The sheaf gluing condition enforces local-to-global consistency, but the priority ordering is a global hand-tuned device that lives outside the sheaf itself.
Presents itself as a 'coherent system' yet dedicates 23 edge-case resolutions to the inevitable local failures, so coherence is achieved through exceptions rather than their elimination.
Humanistic / lived-example grounding coexists with a hard formalist apparatus (Coq, category theory) — a tension between narrative ethics and proof-theoretic rigor.

title: Grothendiecks Universum – Interaktive Visualisierung
category_reason: Reine algebraische Geometrie / Kategorientheorie (Sheaves, Schemata, Yoneda, Topoi, Kohomologie, Dessins d'enfants, Motive) — Grothendiecks mathematisches Universum, keine KI.
thesis: Grothendieks mathematisches Universum ist eine hierarchische Kaskade von Verallgemeinerungen — von konkreten Räumen über Garben und Schemata bis zu Topoi und Motiven — die Geometrie auf reine Struktur (Morphismen, Adjunktionen, Kohomologie) reduziert und damit große Teile der modernen Mathematik in einem einzigen Rahmen vereint.
key_claims: Yoneda-Lemma: ein Objekt wird vollständig von seinen Beziehungen (Morphismen) zu allen anderen bestimmt — 'Struktur durch Beziehung'.
Garben (Sheaves) verallgemeinern lokale Daten, die sich global verkleben lassen; sie sind das Fundament der modernen Geometrie und der Kohomologie.
Schemata ersetzen Punktmengen durch Ring-Bündel — Geometrie wird algebraisch, 'Räume' sind Spektra von Ringen.
Topoi verallgemeinern den topologischen Raum zu 'Universen' von Logik/Geometrie; jedes Topos trägt eine eigene (oft intuitionistische) Logik.
Dessins d'enfants (Belyi) verknüpfen algebraische Geometrie mit Graphen und Zahlentheorie (Absolute Galois-Gruppe).
Motive (Beilinson/Voevodsky) sind die 'Universal-Bausteine' der Kohomologietheorien — ein gemeinsamer Ursprung aller Kohomologien.
visualizations: Canvas 2D (Kategorien, Garben, Diagramme)
interaktive Navigationskarten durch die Konzepte
grafische Schemata (keine 3D-Szenen)

title: Grothendieck — Der Raum: von Schemata zur Geometrie der Formen

key_claims: Delignes Rekonzeption: Der Raum ist definiert durch, was man lokal auf ihm tun kann (Garben/Schnitte), nicht durch seine Punkte.

Das Kontinuum (alle reellen Funktionen / alle Teilmengen von R) ist eine Fiktion: es enthält nicht-konstruierbare Pfade; die Geometrie der Formen ersetzt es durch eine wohlverhaltene, endliche Struktur.

title: What is Group Theory? — An Interactive Visual Guide
category_reason: A pure abstract-algebra visual guide to group theory: symmetries of a square (dihedral group D₄), the four group axioms, Cayley tables, cyclic groups, and subgroups. No AI/ML content.
thesis: An interactive English-language visual guide to group theory starting from the symmetries of a square (the dihedral group D₄ with 8 elements): the user applies rotations and flips to see the symmetries in action, clicks through the four group axioms (closure, associativity, identity, inverses) with live demonstrations, explores the Cayley table (noting the group is non-abelian), plays with cyclic groups via clock arithmetic, and navigates the subgroup lattice of ℤ₁₂.
key_claims: A group captures the idea of symmetry: the square has 8 symmetries (4 rotations + 4 reflections), each of which leaves the square looking the same.

The four group axioms: (1) Closure — combining any two symmetries gives another symmetry in the set; (2) Associativity — (a∘b)∘c = a∘(b∘c); (3) Identity — there is a 'do nothing' element (R₀) that leaves everything unchanged; (4) Inverses — every symmetry can be undone by another symmetry.
The Cayley table (multiplication table) of D₄ is not symmetric across the diagonal — the group is non-abelian (order matters: rotating then flipping ≠ flipping then rotating).
Cyclic groups ℤₙ are the simplest groups: think of a clock with n hours where you add and wrap around; every element generates the whole group.
A subgroup is a subset that is itself a group under the same operation; the subgroups of ℤ₁₂ form a lattice (partially ordered set) where lines connect a subgroup to those it contains.

Group theory underpins physics (particle symmetries), chemistry (molecular symmetries), cryptography (elliptic curves), music theory (transpositions), and Rubik's cube solutions: every time you see symmetry or structure-preserving transformations, there is a group hiding underneath.

visualizations: Square symmetries: a labeled square with 8 transformation buttons (R₀, R₉₀, R₁₈₀, R₂₇₀, Flip H, Flip V, Flip ╲, Flip ╱); click to apply and watch the corners move
