internal_tensions: The file starts with the specific example (D₄) and never generalizes: the reader sees one group in detail but does not get a sense of the vast variety of groups (abelian vs. non-abelian, finite vs. infinite, solvable vs. simple).

The 'What's Next?' section lists applications (physics, chemistry, cryptography, music, Rubik's cube) but does not develop any of them; the connection between the square's symmetries and, say, elliptic-curve cryptography is asserted, not shown.

The cyclic group clock is a good intuition-builder but is presented as a separate example rather than as a special case of the general theory; the relationship between ℤₙ and D₄ (both finite groups, but one abelian and one not) is not drawn.

The file is a visual guide, not a proof: the group axioms are demonstrated with the square, but the reader is not asked to verify associativity for all 512 triples (a∘b)∘c vs. a∘(b∘c); the 'live demonstration' is a single example, not a proof.

title: Interactive Topology Explorer
category_reason: Pure point-set topology: separation axioms T0/T1/T2, countability, hierarchy of topological spaces; no AI/ML connection.
thesis: An interactive sandbox exploring the hierarchy of separation axioms in point-set topology, from T0 through T2 and countability conditions, showing how each axiom adds structure to the notion of topological 'closeness' and which metrizability theorems follow.
key_claims: T0 (Kolmogorov) separates points by open sets: for any two distinct points, at least one has an open neighbourhood not containing the other
T1 strengthens T0: every pair of distinct points can be separated from each other; singletons are closed
T2 (Hausdorff) requires disjoint open neighbourhoods for every pair of distinct points, the standard separation axiom for analysis
Countability axioms (first/second countable) are independent of separation axioms and control metrizability
The hierarchy T2 implies T1 implies T0, and second countability plus T0 implies metrizability (Urysohn)
methods_math: Point-set topology: separation axioms, countable bases, metrizability theorems, Baire category
visualizations: Interactive T0/T1/T2 sandbox with point-pair separation testing; hierarchy map of topological spaces; countability base explorer
internal_tensions: The sandbox simplifies infinite topological spaces to finite point sets, which can obscure the real strength of the axioms (e.g. every finite T1 space is discrete, so finite examples cannot distinguish T1 from T2).

title: Higher Algebra: A Visual Guide
category_reason: Reine Mathematik: höhere Algebra / Homotopie-kohärente Algebra (Monoide, monoidale Kategorien, Spektren, Smash-Produkt, E∞-Ringe, Modellkategorien, Kohärenz, Hierarchie ∞-Kategorien → stabile Spektren → E∞-Ringe → klassische Ringe). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Höhere Algebra studiert dieselben algebraischen Strukturen (Ringe, Algebra), aber in einer Welt, in der Gleichungen nur bis auf (stetige) Deformation (Homotopie) gelten – und diese Homotopien selbst müssen kohärent sein; ein E∞-Ring ist ein kommutativer Ring 'bis auf alle kohärenten höheren Homotopien', präsentiert durch symmetrische/orthogonale Spektren in Modellkategorien, und verallgemeinert klassische kommutative Ringe so, wie Spektren abelsche Gruppen verallgemeinern (𝕊↔ℤ).
key_claims: Ordentliche Algebra: Gleichungen gelten exakt (a·b=b·a). Höhere Algebra: sie gelten nur bis auf Homotopie ('es existiert ein Pfad von a·b zu b·a'), und diese Pfade müssen kohärent sein.
Ein Monoid ist eine Menge mit assoziativer Operation + Einheit; ein kommutatives Monoid erfüllt zusätzlich a·b=b·a.
Ein Monoid in einer monoidalen Kategorie verallgemeinert dies: in (Sets,×) = gewöhnliches Monoid, in (Ab,⊗ℤ) = Ring, in (Spectra,∧) = Ringspektrum.
Eine monoidale Kategorie hat ein Tensorprodukt ⊗ + Einheit, wobei Assoziativität/Unitarität nur bis auf Isomorphie gelten – mit Pentagon- und Dreiecks-Kohärenz.
Ein Spektrum ist eine Folge gezeichneter Räume (X₀,X₁,…) verbunden durch Strukturabbildungen σₙ: S¹∧Xₙ→Xₙ₊₁ ('stabilisierte' Räume).

Das Smash-Produkt X∧Y ist das 'Tensorprodukt' der Spektren; um es streng assoziativ/kommutativ zu machen, braucht man symmetrische/orthogonale Spektren (Day-Konvolution); Lewis' Theorem (1991) zeigt, dass man nicht alle 'netten' Anforderungen gleichzeitig haben kann.

Ein E∞-Ring ist ein kommutatives Monoid in Spektren – 'alles kommutiert bis auf alle kohärenten höheren Homotopien'; die E_n-Operaden (kleine n-Würfel) steuern die Stufen (E₁=A∞ ⊂ E₂=geflochten ⊂ … ⊂ E∞=voll kommutativ).

Eine Modellkategorie hat drei Morphismenklassen (schwache Äquivalenzen W, Fibrationen Fib, Cofibrationen Cof) mit Faktorisierungs- und Liftungs-Axiomen – das 'Workshop-Manual' für konkrete Homotopietheorie.
Die Hierarchie: ∞-Kategorien → stabile (∞,1)-Kategorie der Spektren → E∞-Ringe (kommutative Monoide in Spektren) → Modellkategorien (symmetrische/orthogonale Spektren) → klassische kommutative Ringe.
Die Sphärenspektrum 𝕊=(S⁰,S¹,S²,…) ist der initiale E∞-Ring, analog zu ℤ als initialem kommutativen Ring; π₀(𝕊)=ℤ.

title: Higher Topos Theory — Interaktiver Explorer
category_reason: Main subject is higher topos theory (∞-topoi, Grothendieck topos theory, descent, effective epimorphisms) — pure algebraic geometry / higher category theory with no AI application.
thesis: Higher topos theory generalizes Grothendieck's classical topos theory to the ∞-categorical setting, where objects are not just sets but spaces (∞-groupoids) and descent data are controlled by homotopy-coherent diagrams; this framework unifies algebraic geometry, homotopy theory, and logic under a single categorical roof.
key_claims: An ∞-topos is the ∞-categorical analogue of a Grothendieck topos: it is an ∞-category satisfying higher descent conditions (effective descent for effective epimorphisms).
In classical topos theory, effective epimorphisms are the categorical notion of surjection; in the ∞-setting, they must be homotopy-coherent, which is strictly stronger.
Descent theory — the study of when local data glues to global data — is the engine of topos theory: the topos of sheaves on a site is built from descent data.
Lurie'sHigher Algebra and Higher Topos Theory provide the ∞-categorical foundations that make this framework precise and computable.

step-by-step conceptual explorer with collapsible sections
internal_tensions: The page presents ∞-topos theory as a natural generalization, but the gap between classical 1-categorical topos theory and the ∞-categorical version is enormous — the homotopy-coherence conditions are not a minor technicality but change the entire proof-theoretic content.

title: Topologie der Geschichte (Topology of History) - Interaktiver Explorer
category_reason: It is a German interactive explorer of recurring historical structures (cycles, feedback loops, emergence, path dependence, attractors/phase space, Braudel's time-slices); the dynamical-systems math is applied to history, not to any neural net or ML task.
thesis: A German interactive explorer of recurring structures in history that casts six 'principles' — cyclical dynamics, feedback loops, emergence/self-organization, path dependence, attractors/phase space, and Braudel's time-slices — as live Canvas simulations (with Cliodynamic references to Ibn Khaldun, Spengler, Toynbee, Turchin, and Braudel) to show why history 'rhymes rather than repeats'.
key_claims: Cyclical dynamics: civilizations, economies, and institutions pass through recurring rise-flourish-decline-renewal phases, modeled (Ibn Khaldun's asabiyyah, Spengler, Toynbee, Turchin's cliodynamics) as quasi-periodic oscillations with variable amplitude and damping ('learning').

Feedback loops: positive feedback drives escalation (arms races, bubbles, revolutions) while negative feedback stabilizes (institutions, norms, checks & balances); their interplay with delay and external shocks generates complex historical dynamics.

Emergence/self-organization: complex structures (states, markets, cultures) emerge from simple local interactions of many agents with no central plan, modeled by agent-based simulation with conformity pressure and an innovation rate.

Path dependence: early decisions or chances lock in the whole subsequent course (Lock-in); history is non-ergodic — the path matters, not just the state — with bifurcation points as critical moments (QWERTY, the Reformation, the USSR's collapse).
Attractors/phase space: historical systems converge to stable equilibria, limit cycles, or strange (chaotic) attractors; revolutions are jumps between attractor basins.

Braudel's time-slices: three overlapping temporal levels — longue duree (centuries: geography, climate, mentality), conjunctures (decades: economy, social structure), and events (days/years: politics) — superimpose into the 'history' we experience.

title: Topologische Loecher - Eine interaktive Reise
category_reason: It is a German interactive journey through algebraic topology and topological data analysis (holes, homotopy, simplicial complexes, homology, Betti numbers, persistent homology); machine learning (NN latent space, GANs, OOD) is only one of six application domains, not the focus.
thesis: A German interactive 8-part journey through the mathematics of topological 'holes': what a hole is (coffee mug = donut), homotopy (a loop that cannot be contracted to a point), simplicial complexes, homology (counting holes as cycles modulo boundaries), Betti numbers, and — the payoff — persistent homology / Vietoris-Rips filtration, which turns 'which holes are signal vs noise' into a persistence diagram (the fingerprint of TDA), closing with applications from neuroscience and biology to machine learning and cosmology.
key_claims: Topology is the art of not being fooled by distortion: a shape's 'form' is what survives continuous deformation (no tearing or gluing) — a coffee mug and a donut are the same (both have one hole), a sphere has zero, and a trefoil / pretzel has three.
The elegant definition of a hole is a closed loop that cannot be continuously contracted to a point; two loops are homotopic iff one can be deformed into the other.

To compute with shapes, discretize into a simplicial complex (0-simplex = vertex, 1 = edge, 2 = triangle, 3 = tetrahedron); the Euler characteristic chi = V - E + F is the first topological invariant (sphere chi = 2, torus chi = 0).

Homology translates geometry into linear algebra: a k-cycle is a closed k-shape, a boundary is a cycle that bounds a region, and a hole is a cycle that is *not* a boundary; H_k = Z_k / B_k and its dimension is the k-th Betti number beta_k.
Betti numbers are the fingerprint of a shape: point (1,0,0,...); S^1 (1,1); S^2 (1,0,1); torus (1,2,1); genus-3 pretzel (1,6,1); they are topological invariants unchanged by continuous deformation.

Persistent homology (the TDA core): grow a ball of radius epsilon around each point (Vietoris-Rips filtration) and track which holes are born and when they die as epsilon grows; long-lived holes (points far above the diagonal in the persistence diagram) are real structure, short-lived ones are noise; the diagram is stable under small data changes and machine-readable.

Applications: grid cells in the hippocampus code a torus; cancer cells show different topological fingerprints; the latent space of neural nets has topology (persistent homology for improving GANs / detecting out-of-distribution data); large-scale cosmic structure (voids/filaments) is quantified by Betti numbers; and sensor-network 'uncovered holes' become beta_1 computations.
methods_math: topological invariants under homeomorphism / continuous deformation
homotopy of loops (contractibility) and the homotopy equivalence of loops
simplicial complexes and the Euler characteristic chi = V - E + F

persistence diagrams (birth/death pairs), persistence, and stability under perturbation
an approximate beta_1 via the Euler estimate b1 ~ E - V + C - T with crude 3-clique (triangle) counting
visualizations: a sticky 8-part nav plus TOC cards, each part an annotated Canvas 2D / three.js / Plotly demo
Part 1: a noisy-ring scatter (point count, noise, ring-fraction sliders) posing 'is this a ring or chance?'

Part 4: a click-to-build simplicial complex (add vertices / edges / faces) with live V, E, F, and chi = V - E + F
Part 5: a cycle-vs-boundary toggle (filled triangle = boundary / no hole vs hollow triangle = cycle-not-boundary / hole)
Part 6: a three.js 3D viewer (sphere / torus / double-torus / pretzel, auto-rotate) with live beta_0, beta_1, beta_2 and chi readouts

Part 7: a Vietoris-Rips filtration canvas (epsilon slider plus an animation) with live beta_0 / beta_1, a Plotly persistence diagram (birth vs death for H_0 / H_1), and a Plotly Betti-curves-over-epsilon plot
Part 8: application cards (neuroscience, biology, machine learning, cosmology, time series, sensor networks) plus a written summary of the whole journey
internal_tensions: The piece repeatedly promises 'mathematisch rigoros, stabil' for persistent homology, but the actual beta_1 in the demo is an *approximation* (Euler estimate E - V + C - T with crude triangle counting), not true persistent homology — a gap between the advertised rigor and the toy implementation.

It says a point cloud 'has no holes' and only gains them via the epsilon-filtration, yet also that the answer is stable and machine-readable — the tension being that the answer depends on the chosen epsilon band (scale), so 'which holes are real' is relative to the scale window.

The applications section makes bold, un-argued claims (grid cells 'code a torus'; cancer cells have distinct topological fingerprints; TDA improves GANs) presented as settled fact without evidence; and the piece is general TDA, not specifically about NN/LLM embeddings, so the ML application is thin relative to the topology core.

title: Homotopietheorie — Eine interaktive Reise (nach Ulrich Bunke, 'Introduction to Homotopy Theory')
category_reason: It is an interactive German companion to Ulrich Bunke's classical algebraic-topology/homotopy-theory lectures; the content is pure math with no ML/neural-net focus.
thesis: A 61-'game' interactive companion to Ulrich Bunke's 125-page 'Introduction to Homotopy Theory', retelling the whole subject as one continuous story: from paths and holes, through the fundamental group, covering spaces and the Galois analogy, to the 'machine' (cone/fiber sequences, CW complexes, spectra, spectral sequences) and the capstones pi_n(S^n)=Z (Brouwer), Freudenthal stabilization, and Hurewicz.
key_claims: Two spaces are 'the same' if one can be continuously deformed into the other without tearing or gluing; the real problem is detecting when this is NOT possible, which requires an invariant (pi_0, pi_1, pi_n, H*) that is homotopy-invariant and differs between the two spaces.

pi_1(X) is the first serious invariant: a group, functorial, and homotopy-invariant. Worked catalog: pi_1(S^1)=Z (winding number via path-lifting to R -> S^1), pi_1(S^2)=1 (any loop pulls over a pole), pi_1(T^2)=Z x Z (abelian), pi_1(S^1 v S^1)=F_2 (free, non-abelian — the commutator a b a^-1 b^-1 is nontrivial), pi_1(RP^2)=Z/2 (a half-loop is a genuine loop, a^2=e).

The 'dictionary' Cov(Y) ~ Set with pi_1(Y)-action: covering spaces of Y are exactly the sets carrying a pi_1 action (monodromy); orbits = path components, stabilizer = pi_1 of the lift, transitivity = connectedness, a free transitive action = universal cover. This is a complete lossless translation of covering geometry into algebra.

The same dictionary holds for GALOIS theory, line for line: the fundamental group plays the role of the Galois group, the universal cover the separable closure, and normal subgroups give Galois covers — 'topology and number theory are the same story'.

A homotopy is exactly a natural transformation: the fundamental groupoid Pi(X) is the functor Top -> Grpoids that sends homotopies to natural isomorphisms; categories/functors are the language in which everything else is written.

Naive constructions are NOT homotopy-invariant (the quotient Y/f(X) and the ordinary fiber f^-1(y) both 'jump' under homotopy); the fix is to inflate them into the mapping cone C(f) and the homotopy fiber Fib(f), which makes everything homotopy-invariant and yields long exact sequences 'for free'.

The three basic operations (wedge, smash, suspension Sigma, loop space Omega) plus the adjunction Sigma left-adjoint Omega identify pi_n(X) = [Sigma^n S^n, X] = points of iterated loop spaces; Eckmann-Hilton (two compatible operations force equality and commutativity) is given as a visible proof that pi_n is abelian for n >= 2.

pi_n(S^n) = Z for all n, with the isomorphism given by (co)degree; it is proved via Blakers-Massey -> Freudenthal -> the diagonal being an isomorphism, and yields Brouwer's fixed-point theorem (a fixed-point-free D^n -> D^n map would force the degree to be simultaneously 0 and 1).

Hurewicz: homotopy groups (strong but uncomputable) and homology (weak but computable) agree in the first nontrivial dimension; the proof factors h = epsilon o s (stabilize, then simplify), both resting on Blakers-Massey.

The stable homotopy groups of the spheres pi_k^s are known only up to n ~ 55 — 'the hardest problem in topology'; the whole point of building spectra is to turn the chaotic unstable world into a computable (generalized) homology theory.

A unifying pattern runs through the script: (1) a naive construction is not homotopy-invariant, (2) replace it by an inflated version (cone instead of quotient, homotopy fiber instead of fiber, spectrum instead of a single space), (3) long exact sequences fall out as the computing machines.

thesis: Die Homotopietheorie in der Kurzform: zwei Wege sind homotop, wenn einer stetig in den anderen deformiert werden kann; die Fundamentalgruppe π₁(X) fasst die Schleifen in Homotopieklassen, und π₁(S¹)≅ℤ wird über die Windungszahl berechnet, während ein Schleifen-Rechner die freie Gruppe der Schleifen zeigt.
key_claims: Zwei Wege (mit gleichen Endpunkten) sind homotop, wenn sie stetig ineinander übergeführt werden können, ohne die Endpunkte zu lösen.
Die Fundamentalgruppe π₁(X, x₀) ist die Menge der Homotopieklassen von Schleifen bei Basispunkt x₀, verknüpft durch Konkatenation.

Der Schleifen-Rechner: Schleifen können verkettet, invertiert und reduziert werden – die resultierende Struktur ist (für mehrere Basislinien) eine freie Gruppe.

title: Homotopy Type Theory — Visual Explorer
category_reason: A six-section interactive Plotly-based English-language explorer of Homotopy Type Theory: types as spaces, equality as paths, homotopy, higher paths on a 3D sphere, the univalence axiom, and a 'Rosetta Stone' network graph unifying topology/logic/type theory. Pure mathematics / logic / type theory with no AI or ML content.
thesis: A six-section interactive Plotly-based English-language explorer of Homotopy Type Theory: types as spaces (Bool, ℕ, S¹, ⊥), equality as paths (multiple proofs between the same endpoints), homotopy as continuous deformation of paths, higher paths on a 3D sphere (the ∞-groupoid tower), the univalence axiom (equivalent types are equal), and a 'Rosetta Stone' network graph showing how concepts from topology, logic, and type theory become one and the same in HoTT.
key_claims: In HoTT, every type is a space and every term is a point in that space; Bool has two points (true, false), ℕ is a countably infinite discrete space, S¹ has a base point and a non-trivial loop, and ⊥ is empty.
A proof of a = b is a path from a to b; different proofs are different paths, and the space of equalities between two points can be rich and interesting.
A homotopy is a continuous deformation of one path into another — a 'path between paths' — representing an equality between equalities.
The tower of higher paths (points → paths → homotopies → homotopies between homotopies → …) makes types into ∞-groupoids.
The univalence axiom: if two types are equivalent (there is a perfect two-way mapping with coherence), they are equal; A ≃ B implies A = B. Structure-preserving equivalence is identity.

HoTT unifies three fields: topology (spaces, points, paths, homotopies, homeomorphisms), logic (propositions, proofs, equality proofs, logical equivalence), and type theory (types, terms, identity types, paths between paths, type equivalence).

title: Homotopy Type Theory — Why It Should Be the Foundation of Math
category_reason: Reine Mathematik/Logik: HoTT als mathematische Grundlage – Types as Spaces, Equality as Paths, Univalence, Circle Type, Arithmetic as Paths. Keine ML-Inhalte.

key_claims: Typen sind keine Mengen (Bags of Elements), sondern Räume mit Topologie: Bool ist diskret (2 Punkte, keine Pfade), S¹ hat einen Loop.
Gleichheit ist ein Pfad, nicht ein Bit: verschiedene Berechnungen = verschiedene Pfade = verschiedene Beweise derselben Gleichheit.
Pfade zwischen Pfaden (Homotopien) erzeugen unendliche Tiefe – genau das, was Topologie studiert.

Unvalenz: äquivalente Typen sind gleich. ℤ/2 und {even, odd} sind nicht nur isomorph, sondern identisch.
2+2=4 ist ein Pfad in einem Raum – der Beweis ist ein mathematisches Objekt, das man studieren, komponentieren und invertieren kann.
HoTT wird in Cubical Agda und Lean implementiert – drei Felder (Topologie, Logik, CS) werden zu einer Grundlage.

key_claims: In HoTT, types are spaces, terms are points, and equalities are paths; the identity type a =_A b is a space that can have MULTIPLE inhabitants (many distinct proofs of equality), and J (path induction) is its eliminator — proving a statement means constructing a term of the appropriate type.

N is the inductive type generated by 0 and S with a recursion principle; addition and multiplication are defined recursively on N, and each recursion step is a 'walk one step further' witnessed by definitional equality (refl) — the path from input to output IS the computation.

Z can be built in three equivalent ways: as a coproduct N sqcup 1 sqcup N, as a set-quotient (N x N)/~ with (a,b)~(c,d) iff a+d=b+c, and as the loop space Omega(S^1) ~ Z — the fundamental group of the circle gives the integers a geometric meaning (n = winding around the circle n times).

Q is the set-quotient (Z x Z^+)/~ via cross-multiplication (a*d = c*b), realized as a higher inductive type with path constructors for the equivalence; every operation (e.g. division = multiply by inverse) must be proved well-defined with respect to ~.

R has multiple constructions — Cauchy reals (CauchySeq(Q)/~), Dedekind reals (lower/upper cuts), and a HIT completion with a limit constructor for Cauchy sequences — and the full 'tower of construction' is 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> N -> Z -> Q -> R.

Every equality proof is a path and every proof that two proofs are equal is a homotopy (a 2-path), which gives arithmetic a deeply geometric flavor (path composition = transitivity, inverse = symmetry, homotopy = 2-path).

The Univalence Axiom (A <~> B) <~> (A =_U B) says equivalent types are equal, so different constructions of Z (coproduct vs quotient vs loop space) are literally EQUAL as types, arithmetic defined on one transfers automatically to the others, and the path witnessing the equality IS the translation function.
Division on Q/R requires a witness that the divisor is non-zero, which in HoTT is a function (b = 0) -> 0 into the empty type.

title: Unerreichbare Kardinalzahlen — Interaktive Erkundung der Mengenlehre
category_reason: A German-language interactive exploration of large cardinals in set theory: inaccessible cardinals, measurable cardinals, and their relationship to the consistency strength of ZFC. Pure math/set theory, no AI/ML.
thesis: An interactive German-language exploration of large cardinals: starting from the axiom of infinity (there exists an infinite set), the file builds up the hierarchy of large cardinals (inaccessible, measurable, weakly compact, strong, supercompact) and explains why they are 'large' (they cannot be reached from the empty set by the standard set-theoretic operations) and why they matter (they are equivalent to strong consistency statements about smaller fragments of mathematics).
key_claims: An inaccessible cardinal kappa is an uncountable regular cardinal that is a strong limit: for every alpha < kappa, 2^alpha < kappa. The smallest inaccessible (if it exists) is far beyond the first omega (aleph_0); its existence is independent of ZFC.

A measurable cardinal kappa is an uncountable cardinal for which there exists a non-trivial kappa-additive measure on P(kappa) that vanishes on singletons; equivalently, there is an elementary embedding j: V -> M with critical point kappa. Measurable cardinals are strictly stronger than inaccessible cardinals.

The consistency hierarchy: Con(ZFC) < Con(ZFC + 'there exists an inaccessible') < Con(ZFC + 'there exists a measurable') < ...; each large cardinal axiom increases the consistency strength, and the hierarchy is (conjecturally) well-ordered.

Large cardinals are 'natural' in the sense that they arise from the desire to extend the set-theoretic universe: the axiom of choice + the axiom of infinity give the 'small' universe V; large cardinals extend this to V_kappa, V_M, etc., where the 'large' cardinals play the role of 'infinite' within the extended universe.

The relationship to determinacy: the axiom of determinacy (AD) is incompatible with the axiom of choice but is equiconsistent with a proper class of Woodin cardinals; the 'cardinal-structure of the reals' (the delta^1_n hierarchy) is governed by large cardinals.

The 'naturalness' of large cardinals is a matter of philosophical debate: some set theorists (e.g., Woodin) argue that large cardinals are the 'correct' extension of ZFC, while others (e.g., Gitik) argue that the absence of large cardinals is also a consistent and natural position.

title: Jet Bundles — An Interactive Geometric Introduction
category_reason: A pure differential-geometry / mathematical-physics exposition of jet bundles: their definition as spaces of k-jets, the geometric meaning of derivatives as sections of jet bundles, the chain rule as a pullback map, and applications to PDEs. No AI/ML content.
thesis: An interactive English-language introduction to jet bundles that builds the concept from first principles: a k-jet is the equivalence class of functions with the same Taylor polynomial up to order k, and the jet bundle J^k(E) is the space of all such k-jets over a fiber bundle E; the key insight is that 'taking a derivative' is not a new operation but a projection from J^{k+1}(E) to J^k(E), and the chain rule is the pullback of the total derivative map.
key_claims: A k-jet j^k_f(x) is the equivalence class of all functions germs at x that agree up to order k; it contains all information needed to compute the k-th derivative without knowing the full function.

The k-th jet bundle J^k(E -> M) is a fiber bundle over M whose fiber at x is the vector space of k-jets of sections of E at x; for trivial bundles, J^k(R^n x R) is modeled on R^n x R x (R^{n+1} x ... x Sym^k(R^n) x R).
The total derivative d: J^1(E) -> J^1(J^0(E)) is a natural bundle map; the chain rule for compositions f >> g is the statement that d(f >> g) = df >> dg at the level of jet bundles.
A differential equation of order k is a submanifold (the equation manifold) of J^k(E); a solution is a section s: M -> E whose k-jet extension j^k(s)(M) lies entirely in the equation manifold.
The contact structure on J^k(E) (the kernel of the canonical 1-form) encodes the integrability condition: a submanifold is holonomic (a solution space) iff it is tangent to the contact distribution.
In gauge theory, the curvature of a connection is a section of J^1(P) x_M gl(E); jet bundles provide the natural language for writing gauge-invariant PDEs.
methods_math: fiber bundles, total spaces, projections, local trivializations
Taylor expansion, equivalence classes of germs, jet spaces
total derivative as a bundle map, pullback of maps
differential equations as submanifolds of jet bundles
holonomic vs. non-holonomic submanifolds, integrability conditions
Sym^k(R^n) as the space of symmetric k-tensors (higher-order derivatives)
gauge theory: connections, curvature, jet-bundle formulation of Yang-Mills
visualizations: interactive 1D jet-space explorer: plot a function and watch its 1-jet (point + slope) and 2-jet (point + slope + curvature) as points in R^3 and R^4 respectively
2D surface with a sliding tangent-plane widget: the 1-jet at each point is the tangent plane, visualized as a colored plane that tilts as you move across the surface
chain-rule pullback: two coupled function plots where composing f >> g shows the derivative at the composite point as a pullback of the individual derivatives
contact distribution visualizer: a 3D plot of J^1(R) = R x R x R with the contact plane at each point, showing which curves are 'horizontal' (solutions of a first-order ODE)
equation-manifold slice: a 3D plot of the equation y' = -x^2 in J^1(R), with solution curves projected down to the base
gauge-theory teaser: a fiber bundle over a circle with a connection 1-form, and the curvature as a scalar field on the base (reduction of the jet-bundle picture to a simple case)
internal_tensions: The file is purely mathematical and does not address the common pedagogical objection that jet bundles are 'overkill' for classical ODE courses; the motivation is given as conceptual clarity, not practical necessity.
The gauge-theory application is sketched but not developed; the connection to modern mathematical physics (e.g., the jet-bundle formulation of general relativity) is only mentioned, not worked out.
The 2D visualizations of jet spaces are necessarily low-dimensional; the real power of jet bundles appears in PDEs of several variables, where the geometry is intractable to visualize.

There is a tension between the 'jet bundle as a rigorous formalism' framing and the interactive, hands-on pedagogy: the file oscillates between abstract definitions and concrete examples without fully committing to either.

key_claims: The JN is not 'something in which nothing exists' (that would be contradictory) but a state with no constraints at all
Without rules, there is no restriction on existence — no physical law, no logic, no time that could prevent it
Without time, 'possible' and 'actual' collapse: what is possible simply is
The JN is not the quantum vacuum (which has spacetime and quantum mechanics), not the classical nothing (which implicitly forbids existence)
From the JN, anything can emerge: matter, space-time, natural laws, mathematical structures, other universes, consciousness

title: Johnson–Lindenstrauss · visuell
category_reason: Main subject is the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma in metric geometry and the probabilistic method — a pure mathematics theorem. While JL has ML applications, the page is about the theorem and its proof, not about ML.
thesis: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma states that any set of n points in a high-dimensional Euclidean space can be projected into a space of dimension k = O(log n / ε²) such that all pairwise distances are preserved within a factor of (1 ± ε); the proof rests on measure concentration on the sphere (Lévy's inequality) and a union bound over all n²/2 pairs, and the log n bound is essentially tight by a volume-packing argument.
key_claims: A random rank-k orthogonal projection, scaled by √(d/k), preserves all pairwise distances of n points within (1 ± ε) with positive probability, provided k ≥ K(ε)·log n.

The key ingredient is Lévy's inequality / the isoperimetric inequality on S^{n−1}: the projection length of a random vector concentrates exponentially around its median, with deviation probability ≤ 4·exp(−nε²).

The union bound over all n(n−1)/2 pairs converts the single-pair concentration into a simultaneous statement: the failure probability is at most 2n(n+1)·exp(−nτ²), which is < 1 when k is large enough.
The log n bound is tight up to constants: a ball of radius 2 in ℓ₂^k contains at most 4^k vectors with pairwise distance ≥ 1, so n separated points require k ≥ log n / log 4.

The original 1984 paper by Johnson and Lindenstrauss was not about dimensionality reduction — it was about Lipschitz extensions into Hilbert space, and the famous lemma was a 'simply stated elementary geometric lemma' on page 2.
methods_math: Lévy's inequality / isoperimetric inequality on the sphere
visualizations: canvas: hero animation of point cloud collapsing onto a plane
canvas: log-scale comparison of exact (n−1) vs JL (log n) dimension
canvas: interactive 3D→2D projection with drag-to-orbit, random plane, distortion readouts

canvas: packing bound 4^k visualization
canvas: finale proof animation
internal_tensions: The page presents the JL lemma as a clean, solved problem, but the constants in K(ε) are far from optimal and the lemma says nothing about which random projection to use in practice (the existence proof is non-constructive).
The 'original context' section reveals that the lemma was a tool, not the point — this historical nuance complicates the common narrative that JL is 'about' dimensionality reduction.

title: Geometrische Visuelle Halluzinationen — Interaktiv
category_reason: Physics/dynamical-systems account of hallucination patterns in the biological visual cortex, not ML.
thesis: Geometric visual hallucinations (Kluver's form constants) arise from Turing-type pattern formation in V1, and the log-polar retino-cortical map turns simple cortical activity stripes into spirals, tunnels, and grids in the visual field.
key_claims: Kluver (1920s) classified hallucination patterns under mescaline into 4 form constants: tunnels/funnels, spirals, grids/honeycombs, spiderwebs.
Ermentrout & Cowan (1979) gave the first mathematical model: V1 activity forms periodic patterns via Turing instability (bifurcation + group theory).
Bressloff et al. (2001) added orientation selectivity and Euclidean symmetry (shift-twist), explaining all Kluever form constants.
The retino-cortical map is x = ln(r), y = theta: circles map to vertical lines, rays to horizontal lines, spirals to diagonal lines; so V1 stripes appear as spirals/tunnels/grids.
The dispersion relation lambda(q) = -1 + mu * w_hat(q) decides which wavelength destabilizes first; short-range excitation = activator, long-range inhibition = inhibitor.
Goldenfeld (2018): we do not constantly hallucinate because sparse inhibitory connections suppress spontaneous patterns, which drugs then disturb.
methods_math: Euclidean group E(2) and axial subgroups (planforms)
visualizations: Canvas pattern generators comparing V1 (cortex) vs the visual field via inverse log-polar mapping, with a pattern selector and wave-number slider; a Plotly dispersion-relation plot with excitability and inhibition-range sliders; a live 2D Wilson-Cowan simulation (start/reset/speed); and planform tabs (rolls/squares/hexagons).
internal_tensions: It is a physics/model of a biological system, not of an artificial network — the 'neural computation' citations do not make it ML.
The stochastic-Turing suppression account (why we don't always hallucinate) is a proposed mechanism, not fully established.

title: Chain Complexes — From Zero to Homology (Interactive Visual Guide)
category_reason: Reine Mathematik: Kettenkomplexe & Homologie von Grund auf (abelsche Gruppen, Module, Randoperatoren, Ketten-/Kokettenkomplexe, Homologie, Kettenabbildungen, doppelte Komplexe, Euler-Charakteristik). Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Kettenkomplexe sind Folgen von Modulen, verbunden durch Randoperatoren mit der Goldenen Regel ∂∘∂=0; aus ihnen entsteht Homologie Hₙ=Zₙ/Bₙ (Zyklen modulo Ränder), die die 'Löcher' eines Raums misst – und alles (Simplicial-, Singular-, de-Rham-Kohomologie, Gruppenkohomologie, elliptische Komplexe) ist ein Spezialfall dieses einzigen Musters.
key_claims: Eine abelsche Gruppe ist eine Menge mit einer Operation '+', die abgeschlossen, assoziativ, mit Einheit, inversen und kommutativ ist (die Kommutativität macht sie 'abelisch').
Ein Modul ist die Verallgemeinerung eines Vektorraums, wo die Skalare aus einem Ring R (statt einem Körper) kommen; ein ℤ-Modul ist exakt eine abelsche Gruppe.
Die Goldene Regel der homologischen Algebra: ∂∘∂=0 – der Rand eines Randes ist nichts (z.B. der Rand einer Kante ist v₁−v₀; der Rand dessen ist 0).
Ein Kettenkomplex ist eine Folge ⋯→C₃→C₂→C₁→C₀→0 mit ∂ₙ∘∂ₙ₊₁=0; ein Kokettenkomplex läuft in die andere Richtung (Indizes steigen).
Homologie Hₙ=Zₙ/Bₙ misst 'Löcher': Zₙ=ker ∂ₙ (geschlossene Zyklen), Bₙ=im ∂ₙ₊₁ (echte Ränder); der Quotient zählt die nicht-trivialen Zyklen.
Kettenabbildungen sind 'Übersetzungen' zwischen zwei Kettenkomplexen, die die Randoperatoren respektieren (kommutive Quadrate) und so induzierte Abbildungen auf der Homologie definieren.
Doppelte Komplexe sind 2D-Gitter; der totale Komplex summierst entlang der Anti-Diagonalen (Tot(D)ₙ=⊕_{p+q=n} D_{p,q}).
Die Euler-Charakteristik χ=Σ(−1)ⁱ dim Cⁱ ist invariant (z.B. Würfel: 8−12+6=2; Torus: 0) und verallgemeinert auf jeden Kettenkomplex.

Der Übergang von 'topologische Löcher' zu 'algebraische Quotienten' ist der springende Punkt – die Verbindung wird an Beispielen gezeigt, aber der Satz von der Homotopie-Invarianz wird nicht bewiesen.

title: Der Kult der statistischen Signifikanz — very simple

thesis: A deliberately simple German-language explanation of why the 'cult of statistical significance' — the practice of treating p < 0.05 as a binary gate for what counts as a real effect — is harmful to empirical science, following the critique of Ziliak & McCloskey (2008/2009), with intuitive analogies and simple numerical examples.
key_claims: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what was observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true — it is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that the result is a fluke.
The 0.05 threshold is arbitrary (chosen by Fisher as a convenient convention, not a logical boundary); effects with p = 0.049 are not 'real' while effects with p = 0.051 are not 'fake'.

Binary significance testing discards the magnitude of the effect and the strength of the evidence: a p-value of 0.04 with a tiny effect size is published, while a p-value of 0.06 with a large, important effect is ignored.

The correct question is not 'is the effect statistically significant?' but 'how large is the effect, and how precise is our estimate?' — confidence intervals and effect sizes convey more information than p-values.
The 'very simple' framing targets a non-specialist audience (students, journalists, policy makers) who encounter p-values in news reports and need to understand what they do and do not tell them.

title: Laws of Form — Interactive Explorer
category_reason: Interactive exposition of G. Spencer-Brown's 'Laws of Form' (calculus of indications) — formal logic / foundations, with no machine-learning application.
thesis: Spencer-Brown's calculus of indications derives all of Boolean logic from a single mark and two axioms (Law of Calling, Law of Crossing) built on the primordial act of making a distinction; its most radical extension, 're-entry' (f = ⌐(f)), has no fixed Boolean solution and instead oscillates — an 'imaginary' third value analogous to √(−1) that anticipates time, cybernetics and self-reference.
key_claims: Everything begins with a distinction: drawing a boundary splits the void into a marked (inside) and an unmarked (outside) state; the mark '⌐' is both the act and the name of the marked state.
Law of Calling (idempotence): ⌐⌐ = ⌐ — repeating a distinction side-by-side doesn't change its value (any number of adjacent marks = one).
Law of Crossing (double negation): ⌐(⌐) = ∅ — crossing a boundary twice returns to the start; even depth = unmarked, odd depth = marked.
The calculus is equivalent to Boolean algebra: mark = True, unmarked = False, cross = NOT, adjacency (calling) = OR; e.g. ⌐(⌐p ⌐q) = p AND q, ⌐p q = p → q.

Re-entry: f = ⌐(f) has no fixed Boolean value (if f is marked then ⌐f is unmarked, contradiction); Spencer-Brown resolves it by letting f oscillate over time — a third, 'imaginary' value analogous to √(−1).
Re-entry is the seed of time, oscillation and self-reference, anticipating cybernetics, autopoiesis and the foundations of computation; 'the universe begins with a distinction'.
methods_math: calculus of indications / Spencer-Brown notation (marked ⌐ / unmarked ∅)
Boolean algebra (NOT, OR, AND, NOR, NAND, implication, equivalence)
visualizations: DOM/interactive (no canvas): a distinction box toggling void↔marked; a Law-of-Calling mark-count slider condensing n marks to one; a Law-of-Crossing nesting-depth slider with nested colored depth rings and even/odd result; a combined expression evaluator with step-by-step reduction; a Boolean-logic panel with p/q toggles and a live operation table; a re-entry panel with a time-step slider and auto-oscillate toggle showing the marked/unmarked history trail.
internal_tensions: The re-entry 'oscillation = imaginary value' move is a non-standard, interpretive extension of a two-valued logic; it is often read as suggestive rather than a rigorous logic (the 'imaginary' third value is a metaphor, not a constructed field).

The grand claim that one symbol + two axioms 'derive the entirety of Boolean algebra' is accurate for the static calculus, but the philosophical overreach ('the universe begins with a distinction', foundations of computation) is much harder to defend.

The even/odd-depth reading of crossing quietly assumes a consistent time-orientation; re-entry shows exactly where that assumption breaks, which the doc treats as a feature (oscillation) rather than an inconsistency to resolve.

title: Making It Explicit — Interaktive Reise durch Brandoms Meisterwerk
category_reason: It is a German interactive journey through Robert Brandom's 'Making It Explicit' (inferentialism, norms, deontic scorekeeping, anaphora, de re/de dicto, objectivity); it is a philosophy-of-language piece with no ML/neural-net focus.
thesis: An interactive German journey through Robert Brandom's 'Making It Explicit': it is driven by the question of what makes a system genuinely discursive, and argues that meaning is inferential (the role a content plays in inferences) and that discursive practice is grounded in 'deontic scorekeeping' — the bookkeeping of commitments and entitlements that participants track for one another — from which objectivity (norms pointing beyond any individual) and the anaphoric (not substantial) character of truth and reference follow.
key_claims: The driving question is what separates a genuinely discursive (reason-giving) practice from a mere stimulus-response system (the thermostat-vs-reporter contrast): a system is discursive when its responses are subject to the give-and-take of reasons.

Norms are the 'invisible architecture of the mind': a rule is not a regularity (the rule-regress / Wittgenstein point, and the gerrymandering contrast show that mere regularity is not normativity), and what is normative is the entitlement to count a response as correct.

Inferentialism: the meaning (content) of a claim is its role in inferences — you 'build meaning through inferences'; logic has an expressive role (it is not a body of truths but the machinery for tracking the consequences of commitments).
Deontic scorekeeping is the heart of the book: a discursive practice is the game of tracking one another's commitments and entitlements; an interactive scorekeeper 'game' lets the reader play it.

Perception and action are the inputs and outputs of the scorekeeping: the thermometer-vs-reporter (Sellars) contrast shows the difference between a mere indicator and a reason-giving reporter, and practical inference is the move from a belief to an action.

Truth and reference are ANAPHORIC, not substantial: truth is best understood via the prosentence operator (a device that repeats/endorses a prior assertion), and reference is likewise anaphoric rather than a direct 'naming' relation.

Substitution is how sentences are decomposed: Frege's substitution test (contexts that preserve truth value) identifies the parts a sentence is built from; anaphoric chains link subsequent references back to what was asserted.

De re vs de dicto are the two perspectives on attribution (attributing to an object vs to a description); and objectivity is how norms point beyond any single scorekeeper — the 'objectivity proof' shows that a practice with mutual scorekeeping is answerable to norms no individual sets.
The closing move is 'who we are': the scorekeeping picture is offered as an account of what it is to be a discursive agent.

title: Mannigfaltigkeiten — Interaktiv verstehen (Wie misst man auf einer gekrümmten Welt?)
category_reason: It is an interactive German teaching companion to a differential-geometry/analysis course (Kühnel, Uni Freiburg) on manifolds; the whole content is pure math with no ML/neural-net focus.
thesis: A 58-demo interactive companion to Kühnel's 'Einführung in Mannigfaltigkeiten' that builds, step by step, the complete apparatus for doing analysis (derivatives, integrals, extrema, area, geodesics) on spaces that are only locally like R^n — and answers a concrete guiding question at the end: can you comb a hedgehog (the Hairy Ball theorem)?
key_claims: A (smooth) manifold is a Hausdorff, second-countable space that can be covered by homeomorphisms (charts) onto open subsets of R^n whose transition maps are C^k; 'smooth' means the chart changes are smooth (Def 4.1).

The tangent space T_xM is defined abstractly as derivations: linear maps D with D(fg)=f(x)D(g)+g(x)D(f); the Leibniz rule alone characterizes directional derivatives, so a vector needs no ambient space, and {partial_i} is a basis with dim T_xM = dim M (Def 5.4, Lemma 5.6).

Integration on a manifold is done only on n-forms, not functions, because an n-form transforms under a chart change exactly by det(d psi) — the Jacobian factor is built in, which is what makes the integral chart-independent (Prop 8.5).

The exterior differential d is uniquely characterized by four axioms, the crucial one being d o d = 0 (cancellation of the symmetric second-derivative matrix against the antisymmetric wedge); on R^3, d on 0/1/2-forms is grad/rot/div (Satz 8.10).

A manifold is orientable iff it admits a nowhere-vanishing volume n-form (Satz 10.3); in particular R P^n is orientable iff n is odd, and all complex curves / CP^n are orientable (non-orientability is a purely real phenomenon).

Stokes' theorem int_M d omega = int_(dM) i^* omega is the fundamental theorem of calculus in every dimension, and the three classical theorems (HDI n=1, Green n=2, Gauss/Divergence n=3) are its special cases; compact support is essential (else 'mass escapes to infinity').

Hairy Ball theorem (Satz 2.8): every continuous vector field on S^2 has a zero; the proof assumes a nowhere-zero field, normalizes it, builds the homotopy H(u,t)=cos(pi t)u+sin(pi t)Y(u) from id to the antipodal map, and via Stokes obtains the contradiction 4 pi = -4 pi. Consequence: even-dimensional spheres cannot be combed, odd-dimensional ones can.

The tangent bundle TM is always orientable (its transition determinants are |det d psi|^2 > 0), so T S^2 is not diffeomorphic to S^2 x R^2 — the first genuinely topological (bundle-theoretic) fact of the script.

With a Riemannian metric one measures length/angle/volume; the Laplace operator Delta = d delta + delta d recovers the classical Laplacian on R^n, and the Green's-formula corollary says: on compact M every harmonic function is constant and Delta u = f is solvable only if f has zero mean.

title: Miller-Rabin Primzahltest – Interaktiv erklärt
category_reason: Interactive exposition of a probabilistic primality test from number theory / modular arithmetic; no AI focus.
thesis: Miller-Rabin is a probabilistic primality test: write n−1 = 2^s·d, and for a base 'witness' a, if a^d ≡ 1 (mod n) or some a^(2^r·d) ≡ −1 (mod n) then n passes as 'probably prime'; otherwise a single witness proves n composite, with error bounded by (1/4)^k over k rounds.
key_claims: Decompose n−1 = 2^s·d with d odd; s counts the squaring steps, d is the odd start.
n is definitely composite if no term in the sequence a^d, a^(2d), …, a^(2^s·d) mod n equals 1 or −1; a single such witness 'proves' compositeness.
A single witness can 'be wrong' with probability at most 25%; k independent rounds drop the error to (1/4)^k.
Modular exponentiation is done by repeated squaring (binary exponent decomposition).
The geometric picture: numbers 0…n−1 on a clock/circle; primality corresponds to predictable squaring jumps toward 1 or passing −1.
visualizations: Canvas 2D 'Zahlenkreis mod n': the relevant residues plotted on a circle with 0, 1, n−1(≡−1) marked, arrows tracing the squaring sequence a^d→a^(2d)→…; DOM: decomposition tree, witness sequence pills (colored for 1 / −1 / suspicious), multi-round witness results, hand-calculation detail.
internal_tensions: The 'clock' visualization is a loose analogy — modular squaring is not literal spatial motion on the circle, and it does not capture the group-theoretic (quadratic-residue) structure that actually drives the test.

Frames the test in terms of 'Zeugen' (witnesses) that 'interrogate' the number, a personification that elides the deterministic-vs-probabilistic subtlety (the test never 'proves' primality, only compositeness).
The example n=221=13·17 with a=174 is chosen to expose a composite; the 'Zufällig' candidate list mixes primes and composites but the random pick may silently land on an even/invalid number.

title: Modelltheorie — Interaktive Einführung
category_reason: German interactive introduction to model theory (a branch of mathematical logic): structures, languages, satisfaction, elementary equivalence, compactness, completeness, and the Löwenheim-Skolem theorems. Pure mathematical logic with no AI/ML content.
thesis: A German-language interactive introduction to model theory: the branch of mathematical logic that studies the relationship between formal languages (sentences built from symbols and rules) and their models (mathematical structures that satisfy those sentences). The key results — compactness, completeness, and Löwenheim-Skolem — are presented as surprising consequences of the limitations of first-order logic, with interactive examples for the user to explore.
key_claims: A structure M = (M, ·, +, 0, 1, ...) interprets the symbols of a language L and assigns them meaning; a sentence φ of L is 'true in M' (M ⊨ φ) if the interpretation makes it so; the theory of M is the set of all sentences true in M.

Two structures are elementarily equivalent (M ≡ N) if they satisfy exactly the same first-order sentences; elementary equivalence is weaker than isomorphism — there are non-isomorphic structures that are elementarily equivalent (e.g., the rationals and the reals are elementarily equivalent as ordered fields, by the completeness theorem + model of Th(Q)).

The compactness theorem: if every finite subset of a set of sentences Σ is satisfiable, then Σ itself is satisfiable; this leads to counterintuitive results such as the existence of non-standard models of arithmetic (with 'infinite' natural numbers) and the existence of an ordered field between the rationals and the reals.

The completeness theorem (Gödel 1930): a sentence is logically valid (true in all structures) if and only if it is provable from the axioms of first-order logic; this is a syntactic/semantic bridge that does not hold for second-order logic.

The Löwenheim-Skolem theorems: if a countable first-order theory has an infinite model, it has a countable model (downward LS) and a model of every infinite cardinality (upward LS); this means first-order logic cannot pin down the cardinality of a structure, even for the natural numbers.
methods_math: first-order logic: syntax (terms, formulas, sentences) and semantics (structures, satisfaction)
Tarski's definition of truth (satisfaction relation M ⊨ φ)
compactness via the ultraproduct construction or via the completeness theorem
Gödel completeness theorem: syntactic provability = semantic validity
Löwenheim-Skolem theorems via the downward and upward constructions
visualizations: structure explorer: a small finite structure (e.g., a graph with 5 nodes and some edges) with the user able to toggle edge presence; first-order sentences are evaluated live (e.g., 'every node has degree ≥ 2', 'there exists a triangle')

compactness demo: a set of sentences Σ is built incrementally; the user can check that every finite subset is satisfiable (with a small model shown) and then see the full model that compactness guarantees

Löwenheim-Skolem animation: a large uncountable model is shown, and the 'downward' construction is animated to show how a countable submodel is extracted; the user can see which elements are 'kept' and which are 'dropped'
elementary equivalence gallery: pairs of structures (e.g., (Q, <) and (R, <), (N, +, ·) and a non-standard model) shown side-by-side with the sentences they agree/disagree on
internal_tensions: The interactive examples use finite structures for intuition, but the key theorems (compactness, LS) are about infinite structures; the finite examples are suggestive but do not capture the actual content of the theorems.

The page presents model theory as a self-contained branch of logic, but its applications (e.g., to database query optimization, program verification, and the foundations of physics) are not mentioned, which may make the subject seem purely abstract to a practical reader.

title: Kohärente Verschiedenheit — interaktive Reise
category_reason: An interactive mathematical-philosophical journey from Spencer-Brown's distinction through relation, locality, sheaves, infinity-coherence, to topos — a structural lens, not an AI/ML paper.
thesis: A step-by-step visual derivation that 'coherent difference' — not space — is fundamental: starting from a bare distinction (Spencer-Brown), then relation, locality, sheaf gluing (local -> global), infinity-coherence (equality becomes equivalence with higher coherences), and finally the idea that an 'object' can be the coherent net of its manifestations, all the way to a topos as a whole local mathematical world. It is explicitly a didactic model / shared structural lens, not an established ontology.
key_claims: Spencer-Brown's distinction (A|B) is the minimal starting point: a boundary makes two sides distinguishable but says nothing about how they connect.
Relation (R(A,B)) then locality (a neighbourhood U(x)) organize connections into a structure; locality here is still more metric than general topology.
A (ordinary) sheaf: local data s_i in F(U_i) must be equal on overlaps (s_i|_{U cap V} = s_j|_{U cap V}) to glue into a global section.

infinity-sheaves / infinity-coherence replace strict equality by equivalence (homotopy): data need not be literally equal, there are equivalences between them, and those equivalences have their own (higher, e.g. 2-dimensional) coherences.

The stronger abstraction: an object = the coherent net of its manifestations (visual/auditory/bodily/spatial), with no privileged center — a philosophical-mathematical model, not a claim that perceptions are literally infinity-sheaves.
A topos is more than a space: it carries a category of objects and an internal (typically intuitionistic, not necessarily classical) logic; 'true' means structurally true in that world.
methods_math: sheaves and gluing (s_i|_{U cap V} = s_j|_{U cap V})
topos theory / Sh(X) (sheaves on X), intuitionistic internal logic

internal_tensions: The file is very honest that the visualizations are 'didactic models' and that the equivalence sign for infinity-sheaves denotes equivalence/homotopy, 'not the same as a merely metric nearness' — the risk is over-reading pretty diagrams as literal formalisms.

It runs a continuum from very concrete (Spencer-Brown boundary, metric neighbourhoods) to very abstract (topos with internal logic) that are related only by analogy; the final step explicitly says the thesis is 'a common structural lens under which the discussed theories become comparable', not an established ontology.

The shift from 'equations of motion' (Newton, Einstein) to 'rules of update' (cellular automata) changes the scientific question from 'what is the equation?' to 'what is the rule, and why this rule and not another?'

title: Ologs – Interaktive Reise durch Spivak & Kent (2012)
category_reason: It is a German interactive companion to Spivak & Kent (2012), 'Ologs: A Categorical Framework for Knowledge Representation'; although knowledge representation is a classical AI sub-field, the content here is pure categorical logic (categories, functors, limits, database schemas) with no ML/neural-net component.
thesis: An interactive German journey through Spivak & Kent (2012), 'Ologs: A Categorical Framework for Knowledge Representation': it argues that scientific and corporate knowledge is trapped in 'silos' of prose that cannot be precisely linked, and that ologs — labelled categories / sketches — give a language that is both human-readable and machine-precise, serving as database schemas, expressing primitive recursion, and being composable between authors via functors.
key_claims: The problem ologs solve: knowledge is stored in prose 'silos' that cannot be precisely linked; we need a language that is human-readable AND machine-precise and can translate ideas between different authors.

The idea is to use the language of category theory: boxes for concepts (types), arrows for functional relations (aspects), and commutative diagrams for facts; a basic olog is exactly a category with English labels, where each element has a meaning.
An olog-arrow IS a function between sets: every source element has exactly one arrow out, no source may point at two targets (no ambiguity), but two sources may point at the same target.

Categories = graphs plus path-equivalences: arrows compose, and two different paths A -> C may be declared equal (a commutative diagram); this is what 'pins down' meaning and is the key difference from RDF/OWL/semantic nets.

Building blocks: a Type is a box labelled with a noun ('a person', 'a woman', 'a pair (a,b) where ...'); an Aspect is an arrow = function ('a woman is a person'); a Fact is a commutative diagram ('the female parent of a person is their mother' = two paths are equivalent); good style has boxes start with 'a/an' and arrows form English sentences.
Instances: ologs double as database schemas — a schema (the olog) and a set of instances (a model/functor into Set) are cleanly separated, and primitive recursion can be expressed.

Functors connect ologs (e.g. products, pullbacks, coproducts, pushouts), letting one knowledge model be translated into another and composed, which is what makes them more composable than RDF/OWL/semantic nets in precision.
methods_math: sets, functions, and the definition of a function (total, single-valued, not necessarily injective)
categories, composition, identities, commutative diagrams / path equivalence
labels-as-English (types, aspects, facts) and the discipline of 'good style'
models of an olog as functors into Set (instances as database rows)
products, pullbacks, coproducts, pushouts, and functors between ologs
a fact-tree / metric structure for relating knowledge models
visualizations: a silo-vs-olog toggle (Canvas): prose silos that cannot be linked vs an olog network, with a random-seed slider
a function-building game: drag arrows from set A to set B and check whether the result is a valid function (|A|, |B| sliders)
a category/path-building demo: click arrows to build paths, and reveal the commutative area when two paths are declared equal
a live olog editor ('family'): sliders resize the 'woman' and 'person' boxes and a checkbox toggles the 'mother = female parent' fact (the checkmark appears when the diagram commutes)
an instances / database-schema demo (olog as schema, models as rows)

internal_tensions: The central tension is precision-vs-readability: ologs try to be both human-readable English and machine-precise category theory, and the piece leans on commutative diagrams to do the 'pinning down' that prose cannot.

It is explicitly positioned against RDF/OWL/semantic nets as more precise and composable, but that is a comparative claim about expressivity/compositionality, not an empirical one — the value is structural, and the piece is a categorical-logic tutorial rather than a KR system.
Though knowledge representation is a long-standing AI sub-field, this particular artefact has no learning/neural content; the 'AI' is classical symbolic/compositional knowledge modelling.

title: Betriebssysteme — Interaktive Erkundung
category_reason: A German-language interactive explainer for operating systems: processes, threads, memory management (virtual memory, paging), scheduling algorithms, file systems, and the kernel/user-space boundary. Pure CS, no AI/ML.
thesis: An interactive German-language explainer for operating systems that walks through the core abstractions (process, thread, virtual memory, file) and the key algorithms (scheduling, page replacement, disk scheduling) with interactive visualizations. The goal is to make the 'magic' of the OS visible: how a single CPU can appear to run many programs simultaneously, how virtual memory gives each process its own address space, and how the file system organizes bytes on a disk into named files.
key_claims: A process is an instance of a running program: it has its own virtual address space, file descriptors, and system resources; the OS maintains a process table with one entry per process (PID, state, PC, registers, memory map, file table pointer).

A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process: threads in the same process share the address space and file descriptors but have their own stack and PC; user-space threads (N:1 model) are cheaper to create than kernel threads (1:1 model) but are subject to the 'convoy effect'.

Virtual memory: each process sees a contiguous address space (typically 0..2^32-1 or 0..2^48-1), but the physical memory is divided into fixed-size pages (typically 4KB); the page table maps virtual pages to physical frames, and the MMU (hardware) performs the translation on every memory access.

Page replacement algorithms: FIFO (simplest, suffers from Belady's anomaly), LRU (optimal in theory, expensive to implement), Clock/Second-Chance (approximates LRU with a reference bit), and the working-set model (load only the pages the process is currently using).

CPU scheduling: FCFS (first-come-first-served, no aging), SJF (shortest job first, optimal for mean waiting time but requires knowledge of burst length), Round-Robin (time-sliced FCFS, good for interactive systems), and priority scheduling (with aging to prevent starvation).

The file system: a hierarchy of directories and files; each file is a sequence of blocks; the inode (Unix) stores metadata (size, permissions, block pointers); the directory is a table of (name, inode-number) pairs; the free-space management (bitmap, free list, extent-based) determines how new blocks are allocated.

The kernel/user-space boundary: user-space processes cannot directly access hardware or other processes' memory; they must make a system call (syscall) to request a service from the kernel; the syscall is implemented as a software interrupt (e.g., int 0x80 on x86, syscall instruction on x86-64) that switches to ring 0.

internal_tensions: The file is a pedagogical explainer, not a systems-design document; the scheduling algorithms and page replacement policies are presented in their textbook form, without the engineering trade-offs that real OSes face (e.g., CFS in Linux, transparent huge pages, NUMA-aware scheduling).

The 'kernel/user-space boundary' section is important for security (isolation, privilege) but is treated briefly; the file does not discuss modern OS features like seccomp-bpf, SELinux, or capability-based security.

The file is in German and uses OS terminology in its German translation; some terms (e.g., 'Prozess', 'Thread', 'Seite') are consistent, but others (e.g., 'Inode', 'Syscall') are left in English, which is common but can be confusing for learners.
The interactive visualizations are 2D and simplified; real OS behavior (e.g., preemptive multithreading on a multi-core CPU, cache coherence) is not captured by the visualizations.

thesis: An eight-section canvas-based English-language visual guide to HoTT with more technical depth than its sibling hott.html: types as spaces (click to add points), paths as equalities (reflexivity, deformation), path operations (refl, inverse, composition, associativity up to 2-path), higher paths (2-path/homotopy animation), transport along paths (fibers, fibrations), the ladder of homotopy levels (contractible → proposition → set → groupoid → 2-groupoid), the circle S¹ with winding number π₁(S¹) ≃ ℤ, and univalence (step-by-step: types → equivalence → univalence).
key_claims: Types are spaces; elements are points; the identity type x = y is the type of paths from x to y; this is proof-relevant mathematics (different paths = different proofs).
Paths form a groupoid: identity (refl_x : x = x), inverse (p⁻¹ : y = x), composition (p·q : x = z); associativity (p·q)·r = p·(q·r) holds only up to a 2-path, making types ∞-groupoids.
A 2-path (homotopy) is a continuous deformation between two paths; p·p⁻¹ is not literally the constant path but there exists a 2-path deforming it to the constant one.
Transport: given a family of types P: A → Type and a path p: x = y, transport gives p_*: P(x) → P(y); this makes type families into fibrations over the base space.

Homotopy levels stratify types: (-2) contractible (one point), (-1) proposition (any two elements equal), (0) set (all paths between points equal), (1) groupoid (non-trivial paths, trivial 2-paths), (2) 2-groupoid (non-trivial 2-paths); every n-type is also an (n+1)-type.
The circle S¹ has one base point and one non-trivial loop; π₁(S¹) ≃ ℤ (winding number); the encode function transports 0 along the loop applying successor/predecessor.
Univalence: (A ≃ B) ≃ (A = B); two equivalent types can be identified; any theorem proven about A automatically applies to B — isomorphic structures share all properties for free.

title: Sorting with Bialgebras and Distributive Laws — Interactive Explainer
category_reason: It is an English interactive explainer of a category-theory / functional-programming paper (Hinze, James, Harper, Wu & Magalhães, WGP'12) on the categorical structure of sorting algorithms via bialgebras and distributive laws; it is pure category theory / programming-language theory with no ML focus.
thesis: An interactive English visual guide to the categorical structure of sorting algorithms (based on Hinze, James, Harper, Wu & Magalhães, WGP'12): sorting algorithms come in DUAL pairs, and using bialgebras and distributive laws from category theory one can formalize this duality and derive one algorithm from another 'for free' — e.g. insertion sort (a fold/insert) is the dual of selection sort (an unfold/select), and the computational essence shared by bubble sort and naive insertion sort is a single natural transformation called 'swap'.
key_claims: The core thesis: sorting algorithms come in dual pairs, and bialgebras + distributive laws let you formalize this duality and derive one algorithm from another for free.

Folds (catamorphisms) consume a data structure by replacing its constructors with operations; unfolds (anamorphisms) produce a data structure from a seed using a coalgebra; a sort is a map from the initial (unsorted) list mu-List to the final (sorted) list nu-List, and can be built as a fold of an unfold or an unfold of a fold.
Insertion sort is a fold (insert) and its dual selection sort is an unfold (select).

The 'essence' of bubble sort and naive insertion sort is a single natural transformation called swap — it swaps two adjacent elements if they are out of order — and the interactive shows one swap step at a time.

A bialgebra (the interplay of the algebra and coalgebra structures) together with a distributive law captures how the fold and unfold compose, which is what makes the duality rigorous and the derivations 'for free'.
The duality table / summary plot contrasts the paired algorithms and the algebraic data types involved.

title: Spinnenseide ↔ Musik — Visuelle Paper-Tour
category_reason: A visual tour of a 2011 paper using category theory (Ologs/functors) to prove a structural analogy between spider silk and music; no machine-learning application.
thesis: Spider silk (a hierarchical biomaterial) and classical music share the same hierarchical structure, and this can be made a provable functorial isomorphism via Ologs (category-theoretic 'ontology logs'); the paper contributes 'hierarchical Ologs' (nested snapshot boxes) as a new notation.
key_claims: Two very different systems — silk (amino acids → bonds → polypeptides → proteins → nanocomposite) and music (sound waves → stacks → notes → chords → riffs) — share an identical 5-level hierarchy.
An Olog is a category-theoretic map (objects = sets, arrows = functions, functors = structure-preserving analogies); a functor is what makes the analogy a mathematical proof, not a metaphor.
New contribution: 'hierarchical Ologs' — nested boxes (snapshots) making the hierarchy visible; formally a category C with a subcategory H having a tree structure and Ob(C)=Ob(H).
Both systems have a distinguished sub-group: enzymes with an active center (silk) ↔ major chords with a root note (music) — 'distinguished members' bound to a lower level.
Music consonance condition: c·log2(f₂/f₁) ∈ ℤ with c=12 (equal-tempered scale, 12 semitones/octave); all pairwise frequency-ratio entries of a chord being (near-)integral = consonant.
Material analogue: 3–4 hydrogen bonds clustering in β-sheets give super-proportional shear strength (τ_cluster(N) ≫ N·τ_single for N≈3–4); 'more is not better' — over-long clusters fail weakly.
Both systems are damage-tolerant (local defects don't break global function) and show emergent macro-function from pattern-building.
Ologs force rigor: every term in system A must map precisely to a term in B, otherwise it is not a functor — 'superior to usual ontological or heuristic approaches'.
visualizations: Tabbed tour (Idee/Methode/Hierarchie/Formel/Demo/Ergebnisse/Kritik/Fazit) with clickable hierarchy levels; Web Audio API demo playing single frequencies and consonant (C major) vs dissonant (cluster) chords; Canvas: H-bond cluster in a β-sheet (1/3/4/8 bonds with strength bar) and a step-by-step hierarchy build animation (silk boxes ≅ music boxes).
internal_tensions: CRITIQUE 1: protein secondary structure is not always deterministic (same protein can fold multiple ways), threatening the uniqueness of the functional relations in the Olog.
CRITIQUE 2: material properties are objective/messurable while musical perception is subjective/cultural — the functor transfers structure but not the evaluative (aesthetic) content.
CRITIQUE 3: the two Ologs are only fragments of a larger, still-incomplete Olog (anchor object 'a bond'/'a stack' for extension).
CRITIQUE 4: in hierarchical systems function arises from structural arrangement (clustering/stacking), so structure and function are often inseparable (Table 1 deliberately overlaps them).

title: Principia Mathematica — Interactive Explorer
category_reason: An interactive explorer for Russell & Whitehead's Principia Mathematica (1910–1913): propositional logic, type theory, construction of natural numbers from pure logic, and the logicist programme. Pure mathematical logic / foundations, no AI/ML.
thesis: An interactive English-language explorer for Russell & Whitehead's Principia Mathematica: the user can manipulate truth values to evaluate propositional connectives, explore truth tables for tautologies and contradictions, step through the type hierarchy that tames Russell's paradox, watch natural numbers being constructed as classes of classes, build deduction chains via modus ponens, evaluate quantified statements over adjustable domains, and slide through the layers of the logicist programme.
key_claims: Russell & Whitehead showed that just ¬ (not) and ∨ (or) are sufficient to define all propositional logic; every other connective (∧, →, ↔) is definable from these two.

Type theory resolves Russell's paradox ('the set of all sets that don't contain themselves') by introducing a hierarchy of types: a set at level n can only contain members of level n−1, making the paradoxical question ill-formed.

Natural numbers are defined as classes of classes: 0 = the class of all empty classes, 1 = the class of all singleton classes, n+1 = the successor of n; it takes Russell & Whitehead until page 379 of Volume I to prove that 1 + 1 = 2.
Modus ponens ('if p and p→q, then q') is the primary inference rule of Principia; combined with a small set of axioms, it generates all theorems of propositional and predicate logic.
Predicate logic extends propositional logic with ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists) to reason about properties of objects; the truth of a quantified statement depends on the domain and the predicate.

The logicist programme claims that all of mathematics reduces to logic; in 1931, Gödel's incompleteness theorems showed that any consistent system powerful enough to express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, fundamentally limiting the logicist vision.

internal_tensions: The file presents the logicist programme as a coherent grand vision, but Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems (mentioned only in a historical note) fundamentally undermine the claim that 'all of mathematics reduces to logic'; the tension between the Principia's ambition and Gödel's result is not explored in depth.

The type theory section is the most abstract and least interactive: the slider shows type levels, but the file does not let the reader actually try to form the paradoxical set and see why it is rejected; the 'ill-formed' verdict is stated, not demonstrated.

The 1+1=2 reference (page 379) is famous but potentially misleading: the proof is not difficult in isolation; the difficulty is the enormous scaffolding of definitions that must be established first. The file does not make this distinction clear.

The file is an explorer, not a rigorous treatment: the axioms of Principia (e.g., *1.2, *1.3) are not listed, and the connection between the truth-table visualizations and the actual axiomatic system is implicit rather than explicit.

key_claims: Product universal property: for any X with f:X→A and g:X→B there is a unique ⟨f,g⟩:X→A×B with π₁∘⟨f,g⟩=f and π₂∘⟨f,g⟩=g.
Coproduct universal property (dual): for any f:A→X, g:B→X there is a unique [f,g]:A+B→X with [f,g]∘ι₁=f and [f,g]∘ι₂=g.
Duality principle: a product in C is a coproduct in C^op — every product theorem yields a coproduct theorem by reversing arrows.
In Set: product = Cartesian product, coproduct = disjoint union.
Cardinalities: |A×B| = |A|·|B| and |A+B| = |A|+|B|.

title: Pullback — Interaktive Visualisierung
category_reason: German interactive visualization of the pullback construction in differential topology: how a smooth map f: M -> N induces a pullback on functions, forms, and tangent vectors. Pure differential geometry/topology with no AI or ML content.

key_claims: The pullback f* of a function g on N along f: M -> N is simply (f*g)(p) = g(f(p)); it composes g with f and requires no derivative.
For differential forms, the pullback f*(ω) is defined so that the diagram commutes: evaluating f*(ω) on tangent vectors at p equals evaluating ω on the pushed-forward vectors at f(p).
The pullback is contravariant: a map going M -> N induces a map going 'the other way' on forms (N^* -> M^*), reversing the direction of the original map.
The pullback is the universal construction: any map from M to the 'function space' of N factors uniquely through f*, which is why it appears throughout differential geometry.
Pullbacks preserve algebraic structure: f*(g1 ∧ g2) = f*(g1) ∧ f*(g2) and f*(d g) = d(f* g), making them compatible with the exterior calculus.

Primes mod n: for n > 2, the primes are distributed among the residue classes coprime to n (by Dirichlet's theorem, each such class contains infinitely many primes). The visualizer shows the distribution for n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, with the 'missing' classes (non-coprime) highlighted.

title: PRNG Explorer — Visualizing Pseudorandom Number Generators
category_reason: An English-language interactive visualizer for pseudorandom number generators (LCG, xorshift, Middle-square, etc.): it shows the output sequence, the phase space (state transitions), and statistical tests (chi-squared, autocorrelation). Pure CS/cryptography, no AI/ML.
thesis: An interactive English-language explorer for classical pseudorandom number generators: the user can pick a PRNG algorithm (LCG, xorshift128, Middle-square, Park-Miller, etc.), set the seed and parameters, and watch (1) the output sequence as a scatter plot, (2) the state transition map in phase space, and (3) statistical quality metrics (chi-squared uniformity, autocorrelation, serial correlation). The goal is to make the differences between 'good' and 'bad' PRNGs visually obvious.
key_claims: An LCG (x_{n+1} = (a*x_n + c) mod m) is a linear map on Z/mZ; its output quality depends critically on the choice of (a, c, m): Hull-Dobell's theorem gives necessary and sufficient conditions for full period (m is prime or a power of 2, c is coprime to m, a-1 is divisible by all prime factors of m, and by 4 if m is divisible by 4).

Xorshift generators (e.g., xorshift128: x ^= x<<13; x ^= x>>17; x ^= x<<5) are non-linear in the arithmetic sense but linear over GF(2)^n; they have full period 2^n - 1 and pass most statistical tests, but the low-order bits are weak (use the high-order bits).

The Middle-square method (square the seed, take the middle digits) is the first proposed PRNG (von Neumann, 1951); it fails catastrophically: most seeds quickly fall into short cycles or zero, as visualized by the phase-space plot collapsing to a point.

The chi-squared test for uniformity partitions the output range into k bins and tests whether the observed frequencies match the expected uniform distribution; a 'good' PRNG has chi-squared values near the mean (k-1) with the expected variance.

Autocorrelation at lag k measures the correlation between x_n and x_{n+k}; a good PRNG has autocorrelation near zero for all non-zero lags; LCGs show a characteristic 'lattice structure' in the (x_n, x_{n+k}) scatter plot that reveals the linear dependence.

No deterministic PRNG can be truly random; the 'quality' of a PRNG is its ability to pass statistical tests that are hard to distinguish from true randomness, and the 'security' of a cryptographic PRNG is its resistance to state-recovery attacks (next-bit test, hard-core bits).

The Park-Miller minimal standard (a = 16807, m = 2^31 - 1, c = 0) is a multiplicative LCG with full period m-1; it was the de-facto standard for simulation work from the 1960s to the 1990s but is now considered weak by modern standards.

xorshift as a linear map over GF(2)^n, characteristic polynomial, LFSR analogy
