autocorrelation function, lag-k correlation, serial correlation ratio
lattice structure of LCG outputs in k dimensions (Clopper's theorem)
cryptographic PRNG requirements: next-bit test, hard-core predicate, state space size
visualizations: output sequence scatter plot: (n, x_n mod 1) for n = 0..N, with the user able to overlay multiple PRNGs for comparison
2D phase-space plot: (x_n, x_{n+1}) for an LCG, showing the characteristic lattice structure; the number of visible lattice lines reveals the modulus
histogram of output values with the expected uniform distribution overlaid; chi-squared statistic shown in the corner
autocorrelation bar chart: lag 1..50, with the 95% confidence interval; LCGs show a visible peak at small lags
Middle-square collapse animation: watch the state sequence quickly converge to 0 or a short cycle, with the phase-space plot collapsing in real time
Park-Miller vs. xorshift128 side-by-side: the same statistical tests applied to both, with the lattice structure of the LCG clearly visible and the xorshift output appearing 'cleaner'
seed sensitivity: for a fixed PRNG, vary the seed slightly and watch how the output sequence diverges (or doesn't, for bad PRNGs)
internal_tensions: The file presents PRNGs as a purely mathematical/CS topic, but the 'security' section (cryptographic PRNGs) is a different discipline with different threat models; the file does not clearly separate the two.

The statistical tests (chi-squared, autocorrelation) are necessary but not sufficient for PRNG quality; the file does not discuss more powerful tests (e.g., the NIST suite, Diehard, TestU01) or the 'hard-to-distinguish' framing from cryptography.
The phase-space visualizations are for 2D projections; the true state space of a 128-bit PRNG is 128-dimensional and cannot be meaningfully visualized, which limits the insight from the 2D plots.

The file is a visualizer, not a theoretical treatment; the mathematical claims (Hull-Dobell, lattice structure) are stated but not proved, and the connection to number theory (modular arithmetic, primitive roots) is only hinted at.

title: Ricci-Fluss – Visuelle Erklärung
category_reason: A German-language interactive visual explanation of the Ricci flow as a geometric evolution equation: what it is, the heat-equation analogy, curve-smoothing demos, curvature visualization, and its role in Perelman's proof of the Poincaré conjecture. Pure differential geometry / geometric analysis with no AI or ML content.
thesis: A German-language interactive visual explanation of the Ricci flow (∂g/∂t = −2Rᵢⱼ): what it is, how it works (heat-equation analogy for curvature), three canvas demos (2D curve smoothing, surface deformation, curvature coloring), the step-by-step algorithm, singularity analysis, and its role in Hamilton's 1982 program and Perelman's 2003 proof of the Poincaré conjecture.
key_claims: The Ricci flow deforms a Riemannian metric proportionally to the Ricci curvature: regions of positive curvature shrink, regions of negative curvature expand, flattening the geometry over time.
It is analogous to the heat equation but acting on curvature instead of temperature: an unevenly heated metal plate evens out, and the Ricci flow 'evens out' the shape of a space.
Richard Hamilton introduced the flow in 1982; Grigori Perelman used it (with topological surgery at singularities) to prove the Poincaré conjecture in 2003.
In 2D, the analogous flow (curve shortening) smooths any closed curve to a circle — the Ricci flow is the higher-dimensional generalization toward the sphere.
Singularities (where curvature blows up in finite time) are the main obstruction to global convergence; Perelman's key contribution was the surgery procedure that removes them.
The flow converges (after surgery) to a geometry of constant positive curvature, implying the manifold is a sphere (Poincaré).

title: Schleifenraum – interaktiv verstehen
category_reason: It is a German interactive exposition of the loop space Omega(X) and its role in algebraic topology (pointed spaces, loops, the compact-open topology, concatenation, the fundamental group, suspension, the Sigma/adjunction, Eckmann-Hilton, and higher homotopy groups); it is pure algebraic topology with no ML focus.
thesis: A German interactive explanation of the loop space Omega(X): starting from why loops matter and a pointed space (X, x_0), it defines a loop, forms the space of all such loops Omega(X), explains how to topologize a space of functions (the compact-open topology), shows how two loops deform and concatenate (v * w), extracts the fundamental group pi_1(X, x_0), builds the suspension Sigma(X), states the adjunction Sigma left-adjoint Omega (and the Eckmann-Hilton duality), and finally shows how higher homotopy groups arise from iterating Omega.
key_claims: Loops (maps S^1 -> X based at x_0) are the entry point to the higher homotopy groups; the loop space Omega(X, x_0) collects all such loops into a single space whose points are loops.
A pointed space (X, x_0) and a pointed map are the required setup: the basepoint is what makes 'loop' meaningful.
A loop is a continuous map from the circle (or interval with endpoints identified) that starts and ends at x_0.
To make Omega(X) a genuine topological space one must topologize a space of functions; the compact-open topology is the standard choice (subbasis from preimages of open sets on compact domains).
Two loops can be deformed and concatenated: the product v * w means 'run v first, then run w', and this operation (up to homotopy) is what gives Omega(X) its group structure.
The fundamental group pi_1(X, x_0) is the set of free homotopy classes of based loops under concatenation.

The suspension Sigma(X) and the loop space Omega(X) are related by an adjunction Sigma left-adjoint Omega; this is the setting for the Eckmann-Hilton argument (two compatible operations force equality and commutativity, showing pi_n is abelian for n >= 2).
Higher homotopy groups pi_n(X, x_0) are obtained by iterating the loop space: pi_n(X) = pi_1(Omega^{n-1}(X)).

internal_tensions: The load-bearing tension is the adjunction Sigma left-adjoint Omega: looping and suspending are dual operations, and the Eckmann-Hilton theorem (two compatible unital operations force each other to be equal and commutative) is the algebraic heart that makes higher homotopy groups abelian.

Topologizing a space of functions (the compact-open topology) is a subtle step that is glossed rather than fully developed, but it is what turns 'the set of loops' into the topological space Omega(X).
No AI/ML content; this is classical algebraic topology / homotopy theory.

title: Topoi & Sheaves — Where Geometry Meets Logic
category_reason: A seven-part interactive journey through Grothendieck's sheaf theory and topos theory: presheaves, gluing, Grothendieck topologies, sites, topoi, and internal intuitionistic logic. Pure algebraic geometry / category theory / mathematical logic with no AI or ML content.
thesis: A seven-section interactive English-language journey through Grothendieck's sheaf theory and topos theory, from presheaves on open sets through the gluing axiom, Grothendieck topologies on arbitrary categories, sites, the topos as a universe of sets twisted by geometry, to internal intuitionistic logic where truth values become open sets and the law of excluded middle can fail.
key_claims: A presheaf is a contravariant functor F: O(X)^op → Set assigning data to open sets with restriction maps; the 'contravariant' flip means inclusions U→V induce restrictions F(V)→F(U).
A sheaf is a presheaf satisfying two axioms for every covering: locality (sections agreeing on a cover are equal) and gluing (compatible local sections produce a unique global section).

Grothendieck topologies generalize the notion of covering from topological spaces to arbitrary categories: a rule declaring which families of arrows count as 'coverings' determines what 'local' means.
A Grothendieck topos is a category equivalent to Sh(C,J) for some site (C,J); it has products, coproducts, exponentials, a subobject classifier Ω, and internal logic.
In the topos Sh(X) of sheaves on a space X, truth values are open sets of X: a proposition can be 'true on U' and 'false on V', making logic local and intuitionistic (excluded middle can fail).
Sheafification is the left adjoint to the inclusion Sh(C,J) ↪ [C^op, Set], making every Grothendieck topos a left-exact reflective subcategory of a presheaf topos.

internal_tensions: The page mentions étale, fppf, and Zariski topologies as examples of Grothendieck topologies on algebraic objects but never develops them, creating a gap between the elementary sheaf intuition built in sections 1–3 and the advanced algebraic-geometric applications referenced in sections 4–5.

title: Shor's Algorithm Interactive Demo
category_reason: An interactive (partial) exposition of quantum factoring (Shor's algorithm, QFT, period finding) for cryptography; no AI/ML focus.
thesis: TRUNCATED/STUB document (793 lines, no <script>, ends mid-step-6, missing 'step 7: Why It Matters' and all closing tags): it lays out, in structure only, Shor's algorithm as an exponential-speedup quantum factoring method — reducing factoring to period-finding of f(x)=a^x mod N, solved by the quantum Fourier transform — presented across 8 planned interactive steps with CSS and markup but no working JavaScript.
key_claims: Shor's algorithm factors large numbers exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm, threatening RSA.
Factoring reduces to finding the period r of f(x)=a^x mod N (smallest r with a^r ≡ 1 mod N).
Once r is known, factors come from GCD(a^(r/2)−1, N) and GCD(a^(r/2)+1, N) (when r is even and a^(r/2)≠−1).
The quantum part uses superposition + interference; the circuit is |0⟩ → Hadamard (superposition) → modular exponentiation → inverse QFT → measure.
The QFT converts the periodic pattern into a measurable frequency, like a Fourier transform reading the frequency of a note; QFT|x⟩ = (1/√N)Σ_k e^{2πixk/N}|k⟩.
Continued fractions extract the period r from a measurement ≈ j·(Q/r).
Complexity contrast: classical trial division O(√N) (~10^300 ops for 2048 bits) vs quantum O((log N)³) (~10^10 ops).
methods_math: quantum gates (Hadamard, modular exponentiation, measure) / superposition & interference
visualizations: Intended (markup defined, JS absent): quick factoring demo, trial-division log, difficulty-scaling canvas, classical-vs-quantum race canvas, modular-exponentiation table + period canvas, factor-extraction log, step-by-step quantum-circuit canvas (hoverable gates), superposition canvas, QFT frequency-peak canvas + continued-fraction readout, full Shor run. As shipped, none execute (no script).
internal_tensions: The file is incomplete — it presents an 8-step interactive demo but ships only CSS + markup for steps 0–6 (partially), with no JavaScript, no step-7, and no closing </body>/</html>; the interactivity it advertises does not work.
Complexity claims (O(√N) classical) conflate trial division with the actual best classical algorithms (general number field sieve, sub-exponential), a common popularization simplification.
The RSA 'break in minutes to hours' framing elides the engineering/quantum-error-correction gap between algorithmic complexity and a real large-scale quantum computer.

title: Sobolev-Räume W^{k,p}(Ω)
category_reason: Sobolev spaces and weak derivatives — functional analysis / PDE theory; ML appears only as one of eight applications (Sobolev training), not the focus
thesis: Sobolev spaces W^{k,p}(Ω) generalize the derivative via weak (distributional) derivatives, giving a rigorous home for the rough functions that arise as solutions of PDEs; their norm, hierarchy, and embedding theorems (Sobolev, Morrey) explain why enough derivatives force regularity.
key_claims: Weak derivative: v ∈ L^p is the weak derivative of u when ∫ u D^αφ = (−1)^|α| ∫ v φ for all test functions φ — the derivative is pushed onto smooth test functions via integration by parts
H^k = W^{k,2} is a Hilbert space with inner product Σ_{|α|≤k} ∫ D^αu D^αv, useful for projections, orthogonality, and the Riesz representation theorem
|x| ∈ W^{1,2}(−1,1) (weak derivative sign(x)) but ∉ W^{2,p} (second derivative 2δ(0), a distribution); Heaviside ∉ W^{1,p} (derivative δ(0)); |x|^{1/2} ∈ W^{1,p} only for p < 2 in 1D

Sobolev embedding: if kp < n then W^{k,p} ↪ L^q with Sobolev exponent q* = np/(n−kp); if kp = n (critical) it embeds into all L^q, q < ∞; if kp > n (Morrey) it embeds into C^{0,α} with α = k − n/p — enough derivatives force continuity
Lax–Milgram: the weak form ∫ ∇u·∇v = ∫ fv with coercivity a(u,u) ≥ α‖u‖² (via Poincaré) yields a unique weak solution u ∈ H₀¹ — the backbone of FEM and PDE existence
The Sobolev norm grows with frequency: higher ω in sin(ωπx) inflates ‖f'‖ and thus the H¹ norm — Sobolev norms measure smoothness by 'punishing' oscillation
Applications include heat/wave equations, elasticity, Navier–Stokes (Millennium problem), FEM, and — as one card — 'Sobolev training' of neural nets via Sobolev-norm regularization
visualizations: function & weak-derivative plot canvases (vanilla JS canvas 2D) for |x|, sin(πx), Heaviside, |x|^{1/2}, x·sin(1/x)
animated Sobolev-norm bars per derivative order; frequency-vs-H¹-norm plot
nested-ellipses function-space hierarchy; embedding-regime diagram (kp<n / =n / >n) with a position indicator
internal_tensions: A 'Machine Learning' application card (Sobolev training / Sobolev-norm regularization) sits alongside physics applications — an explicit math-for-AI hook, but thin and unelaborated versus the analysis focus

title: Spatiotemporal Composability — Interactive Explainer
category_reason: An explainer for the Cordis software-architecture paradigm: revertible effects (temporal composability) and reactive coeffects (spatial composability) for dynamic component systems. AI agent harnesses are mentioned as one motivating use case alongside VSCode plugins, but the main subject is software engineering / component architecture.
thesis: An interactive English-language explainer for the Cordis paradigm of dynamic software composability, which identifies two orthogonal dimensions: temporal (revertible effects — every side-effect carries its inverse so components can be cleanly unloaded) and spatial (reactive coeffects — components declare dependencies and are automatically activated/deactivated as providers appear and disappear).
key_claims: An effect is modeled as a function Γ → Γ × (Γ → Γ): it transforms the context and returns an inverse; inverses are composed onto an accumulator in LIFO order, so unloading a component perfectly undoes everything in reverse order (Theorem 16 in the paper).

Reactive coeffects: a component declares which coeffects (dependencies) it needs; the runtime classifies every context change as activating, deactivating, or neutral, and components spring to life or gracefully deactivate as providers appear or vanish.
Provider withdrawal is guarded: when a provider is removed, the runtime waits until all dependents finish their teardown before the provider is actually removed (Section 4.2.2).

Every component instance (fiber) moves through a four-state machine: INACTIVE → LOADING → ACTIVE → UNLOADING, with transitions driven by comparing the target view (what should be running) against the committed view (what is running).

Current practice (VSCode, AI agent harnesses) handles dynamic composition by restarting the whole process; Cordis provides a structured, tracked alternative where each component's lifecycle is independently manageable.
The two dimensions (temporal and spatial) are orthogonal: revertible effects solve the 'clean unload' problem, while reactive coeffects solve the 'when should this component run' problem.
methods_math: target view vs. committed view reconciliation
visualizations: Naive vs. Revertible comparison: side-by-side panels showing what happens when a component is removed without vs. with proper effect tracking (leaked resources visible in the naive case)

Revertible effect stack: an animated list of effects (open file, bind port, subscribe, cache) with a forward-order forward stack and a LIFO inverse accumulator; 'Unload Component' runs the inverses in reverse
Reactive coeffect toggle: three provider toggles (Database, Logger, Auth) with dependent components (UserService, etc.) that light up or dim as providers appear/disappear
Component state machine diagram: INACTIVE → LOADING → ACTIVE → UNLOADING with labeled transitions
Full system playground: a live application orchestrating multiple components with real-time state display
internal_tensions: The Cordis paradigm is presented as solving a real problem, but the file does not discuss the performance cost of tracking every effect and maintaining the inverse accumulator — in practice, this bookkeeping can be expensive for high-frequency effects.
The four-state machine is clean but assumes well-behaved components; in practice, components may fail mid-loading or mid-unloading, and the file does not discuss error recovery or partial teardown.

The mention of 'AI agent harnesses' as a use case is intriguing but underdeveloped: the file does not explain what specific composability challenges AI agents face that traditional plugin systems do not.

The 'Theorem 16' reference to the paper suggests a formal foundation, but the file is an explainer, not a proof; the correctness of the LIFO inverse composition (especially with concurrent effects) is asserted, not argued.

title: Takens' Embedding Theorem — An Interactive Exploration
category_reason: Main subject is the Takens embedding theorem from dynamical-systems theory — reconstructing an attractor from a scalar time series via delay coordinates. No ML/AI application is the focus.
thesis: Takens' theorem guarantees that a generic time-delay embedding of a scalar observation from a chaotic dynamical system reconstructs the original attractor up to a diffeomorphism, provided the embedding dimension exceeds twice the attractor's topological dimension — making it possible to recover the full geometry of a system from a single measured signal.
key_claims: For a smooth flow on a compact manifold with topological dimension d, a delay embedding with dimension m > 2d is generically a diffeomorphism onto its image.
The delay time τ must be chosen to decorrelate successive coordinates: too short gives redundant axes, too long gives noise-dominated axes.
The reconstructed attractor preserves the topological invariants (Lyapunov exponents, fractal dimension) of the original system.
The theorem is generic: it holds for almost all observation functions, so a single well-chosen sensor suffices in principle.
visualizations: canvas animations of delay embeddings in increasing dimension
interactive τ and m sliders showing attractor reconstruction quality
internal_tensions: The theorem is a generic existence result — it does not tell you how to find the right dimension or delay time in practice, which remains a data-dependent heuristic.

title: Boundary maps by hand — the pictures
category_reason: Pure algebraic-topology pedagogy (simplices, boundary operator) with no AI application.
thesis: A shape is glued from simplices and the boundary map records each piece's edge/rim/skin; walking through orientation, head/tail, chains, and the animated boundary of a triangle explains why boundary-of-boundary is zero and how Betti numbers count holes.
key_claims: An n-simplex has n+1 corners and lives in n dimensions: point, edge, triangle, tetrahedron.
Ordering vertices by index puts arrows on edges (low to high index), fixing an orientation; swapping two vertices flips the sign.
The boundary of an edge is head minus tail: partial[v_i, v_j] = v_j - v_i.
The boundary of a triangle is built by a ritual — delete each vertex in turn, giving +[v1,v2] - [v0,v2] + [v0,v1] with signs (-1)^i.
partial o partial = 0: at each corner a +1 (one edge's head) meets a -1 (the next edge's tail) and cancels, so a rim has no ends.
Holes are counted by Betti numbers b_n = (# n-simplices) - rank partial_n - rank partial_{n+1}: clusters, loops, hollow voids.
visualizations: Static canvas drawings (four simplices, oriented edge/triangle, head/tail, chain 2a+b-c, partial*partial=0 cancellation) plus one animated canvas stepping through deleting each vertex of a triangle with a pause/play button and a paper-pencil exercise with a reveal-answer spoiler.
internal_tensions: It is deliberately a minimal, intuition/formalism/example teaching doc with no application, so its only open question is why one would learn this (no AI link provided here).

title: Topoi - Interaktive Einführung
category_reason: It is a German interactive introduction to topos theory (the big idea, the three roots, category preliminaries, the elementary-topos definition, the subobject classifier, examples, internal intuitionistic logic, Heyting algebras, and sheaves); it is pure category theory / mathematical logic with no ML focus.
thesis: An interactive German introduction to topoi: it gives the big idea (a topos as a 'universe of sets' that can support its own internal logic), traces the three roots (algebraic geometry, category theory, logic/set theory) that united around 1970, reviews the category preliminaries ('instead of epsilon': monos, products, pullbacks), states the elementary-topos definition, builds up the subobject classifier Omega, walks through concrete examples (Set^2, Set^->, bundles Bn(I), the M2 counterexample), shows that the internal logic is in general intuitionistic (and related to Kripke models), and develops Heyting algebras and the sheaf (geometric) root before a panorama.
key_claims: A topos is a category that behaves like a 'universe of sets' rich enough to support its own internal logic; the three historical roots — algebraic geometry (Grothendieck topologies / sheaves), category theory, and logic/set theory — merged around 1970 into topos theory.
The category preliminaries are recast 'instead of epsilon': injective arrows as monomorphisms, products done categorially, and the pullback (fibre product) as the key construction.
An elementary topos is defined axiomatically (finite limits, a terminal object, exponentials, and a subobject classifier Omega satisfying the Omega axiom).
In Set the subobject classifier is Omega = {0,1}; the defining property is the pullback square, and the general Omega-axiom says subobjects of X correspond to arrows X -> Omega.
Concrete examples: Set^2 (pairs of sets), Set^-> ('sets through time' / arrows), Bn(I) (bundles of sets), and M2 as the canonical counterexample to some tempting generalization.
The internal logic of a topos is in general INTUITIONISTIC, not classical; the logical operations are themselves arrows, and topos logic connects to Kripke models.

Heyting algebras (e.g. the Heyting algebra of open sets of a space) formalize this intuitionistic logic; the sheaf condition (COM) is the geometric root of all of it, and Grothendieck topologies generalize it.

title: Topological Data Analysis — Visual Explorer
category_reason: TDA (Vietoris-Rips, Mapper, Alpha, persistence) applied to generic point-cloud/shape data; ML appears only as a persistence-landscape use-case with no application to neural nets or embeddings
thesis: Topological data analysis extracts the shape of data — connected components, loops, voids — by building simplicial complexes filtered by a scale parameter, and summarizes them with invariants beyond barcodes: persistence landscapes, Euler characteristic curves, Reeb graphs, and the Mapper algorithm.
key_claims: Vietoris-Rips: connect points within distance ≤ 2ε and fill all cliques as simplices; as ε grows, components and loops are born and die (a filtration)

The Mapper algorithm (Singh, Mémoli, Carlsson 2007) projects data through a filter, covers the range with overlapping intervals, clusters each preimage, and builds a graph — a topological 'skeleton' revealing loops, branches, and flares
The Alpha complex is a subcomplex of the Delaunay triangulation (keep simplices with circumradius ≤ α), geometrically more faithful and cheaper than Vietoris-Rips in low dimensions

Persistence landscapes (Bubenik 2015): each interval [b,d] becomes a tent function; λ₁, λ₂, … are pointwise orderings forming a Hilbert space that supports means, variances, and distances — a bridge to statistics and ML
The Euler characteristic curve χ(ε) = V − E + F tracks topological change through a filtration as a compact signature
The Reeb graph contracts each connected component of a level set of f: X→ℝ to a point; its nodes are topology-change (saddle) points — it is the theoretical basis of Mapper
visualizations: per-method tabs, all vanilla JS canvas 2D: Vietoris-Rips with ε-balls and cliques; Mapper (data+intervals → graph); Alpha complex (Delaunay with active simplices); persistence landscapes (tent functions + λ curves); Euler characteristic curve; Reeb graph with an animated level-set sweep
internal_tensions: Framing persistence landscapes as an ML/statistics bridge, yet never applying TDA to any neural network or learned embedding — a gap versus the math-for-AI cluster in this corpus
The Mapper clustering is a naive greedy distance-based clustering rather than the real Mapper's cluster-decomposition; the 'skeleton' is illustrative, not rigorous
All point sets are synthetic (clustered blobs, circle-with-flare); no real datasets are used

Das Manifold-Kapitel erwähnt Neural Nets, aber der Fokus ist reine Mathematik.
thesis: Sechs scheinbar verschiedene mathematische Strukturen – Faltung, Fixpunkte, Entropie, Fourier-Dualität, Mannigfaltigkeiten, Gruppenwirkungen – sind dieselbe Struktur (Representation Theory einer Gruppe) in verschiedenen Verkleidungen.
key_claims: Convolution: jede Messung ist eine Faltung (Auge×Rezeptor, Gedächtnis×Decay, Foto×PSF). Faltungstheorem: Faltung in einem Domain = Multiplikation im Dual.
Fixed Points: Brouwer (geknüllte Karte), Banach (Kontraktion → eindeutiger Fixpunkt), Nash (Gleichgewicht). Iteration einer Map bis f(x)=x.
Entropy: nicht 'Unordnung', sondern 'average surprise'. Compression = Redundanz entfernen. KL-Divergenz = Kosten für falsche Distribution.
Fourier/Duality: jedes Space hat ein Dual, wo harte Probleme einfach werden. Position↔Momentum, Zeit↔Frequenz. Der Transform ist sein eigenes Inverse.

Group Actions: Noether (Symmetrie → Erhaltung). Jede Klassifikation ist Quotientieren durch eine Gruppe.

Unifikation: Convolution ist Gruppenwirkung (Translation), Fourier zerlegt in irreps, Fixed Points sind triviale Orbits, Entropie misst Orbit-Verteilung, Manifolds sind Quotientenspaces. 'It's all representation theory.'

title: Was ist Wahrscheinlichkeit? — Interaktiv erkunden aus 6 wissenschaftlichen Perspektiven
category_reason: A German-language interactive explorer for probability theory from 6 perspectives: Laplace (classical), frequentist (von Mises), Bayesian, information-theoretic (Shannon), quantum (Born), and stochastic processes (Kolmogorov/Markov). Pure math/probability, no AI/ML.
thesis: An interactive German-language explorer for the question 'What is probability?' from 6 scientific perspectives: (1) Laplace/classical (symmetry, ratio of favorable to possible cases), (2) frequentist (limit of relative frequency), (3) Bayesian (degree of belief, updated by evidence), (4) information-theoretic (Shannon entropy, information content), (5) quantum (Born rule, |psi|^2 as fundamental probability), and (6) stochastic processes (Kolmogorov axioms, Markov chains, random walks). Each section has an interactive visualization and a formula box; the final section ties all 6 perspectives together under the Kolmogorov axioms.
key_claims: Laplace's classical definition: P(A) = |A| / |Omega| when all outcomes are equally likely; the dice example (sum of n dice >= target) shows the computation and the distribution of sums.

The frequentist definition (von Mises, 1928): P(A) = lim_{n->inf} h_n(A)/n, where h_n(A) is the number of occurrences of A in n trials; the coin-flip simulation shows the convergence of the relative frequency to the true probability, with a 95% confidence band.

The Bayesian definition: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H) / P(E); the medical test example (prevalence, sensitivity, specificity) shows the posterior probability of disease given a positive test, with a tree diagram; the 'base rate neglect' is highlighted (a 95% sensitive test on a 1% prevalence disease gives only ~9% posterior).

The information-theoretic perspective (Shannon, 1948): H(X) = -sum p_i log2(p_i) is the entropy; I(x) = -log2(p(x)) is the information content of event x; the binary source example shows the entropy curve H(p) = -p log2(p) - (1-p) log2(1-p), which is maximized at p = 0.5.

The quantum-mechanical perspective (Born, 1926): P(a <= x <= b) = integral_a^b |psi(x)|^2 dx; the particle-in-a-box example shows the wavefunction psi_n(x) = sqrt(2/L) sin(n pi x / L) and the probability density |psi_n|^2, with a slider for the quantum number n and the measurement region.

The stochastic processes perspective (Kolmogorov, 1933): probability as an axiomatized measure; the Markov chain P(X_{t+1} = j | X_t = i) = p_ij and the random walk (sum of ±1 steps) show the evolution of probability over time; the diffusion limit (sqrt(t) scaling) is highlighted.

All 6 perspectives satisfy the Kolmogorov axioms: P(A) >= 0, P(Omega) = 1, P(union A_i) = sum P(A_i) for disjoint A_i; the axioms are the common foundation, and the 6 perspectives are different 'interpretations' or 'applications' of the same axiomatic structure.

visualizations: dice distribution plot: a bar chart of the sum of n dice, with the favorable outcomes (sum >= target) highlighted in blue; a canvas shows example dice rolls
coin-flip simulation: a strip of the last 100 coin flips (K/Z), a Plotly chart of the relative frequency over time with the true probability and 95% confidence band

Bayesian medical test: a bar chart of prior vs. posterior probability of disease; a tree diagram showing the population split into sick/healthy and then into test+/test-; the posterior is computed and displayed

entropy curve: a Plotly chart of H(p) = -p log2(p) - (1-p) log2(1-p) for p = 0.01..0.99, with the current p marked; a canvas shows the information content bars for events A and B, and an 'entropy meter' gradient bar

particle in a box: a canvas showing the wavefunction psi_n(x) (blue) and the probability density |psi_n|^2 (red) for quantum number n; a green shaded region shows the measurement interval; the probability in the region is computed by numerical integration

random walk simulation: a Plotly chart of N random walks (colored by hue) with the theoretical mean and 95% confidence band; the final positions are summarized (mean, std) and compared with the theory

summary diagram: a canvas showing the 6 perspectives as nodes around a central 'Kolmogorov Axioms' node, with connecting lines; each node is labeled with the key idea (symmetry, limit, belief, uncertainty, fundamental, axiomatic)
internal_tensions: The file presents 6 'perspectives' on probability as if they are equally valid and complementary, but in practice they are not: the classical and frequentist definitions are special cases or approximations, the Bayesian definition is a subjective interpretation, the quantum definition is a physical law (not a probability interpretation per se), and the stochastic processes definition is the axiomatic foundation. The 'equality' of the 6 perspectives is a pedagogical choice, not a mathematical one.

The quantum section is the most out of place: the Born rule is a postulate of quantum mechanics, not a 'perspective on probability' in the same sense as the others; the file treats it as if it were another interpretation of the same concept, which is a category error.

The frequentist section shows the convergence of the relative frequency, but the 'true probability' is a parameter that is not observable; the file does not discuss the 'frequentist paradox' (the probability of the parameter is not a probability in the frequentist sense).

The file is a pedagogical explorer, not a philosophical treatment; the 'what is probability?' question is a deep philosophical question (the 'problem of the criterion'), and the file does not engage with the philosophical literature (e.g., the frequentist-Bayesian debate, the 'propensities' interpretation, the 'logical' interpretation of Carnap).

title: Warum fühlt sich Raum so an? - Interaktive Erklärung
category_reason: It is a German interactive explainer of a consciousness/perception paper (built on Integrated Information Theory) about why spatial experience feels extended — 'spots', extendedness, the 5 axioms of experience, a grid substrate, and testable predictions — with no ML/neural-net focus (the 'grid' and 'attention = gain increase' are about the brain, not about machine learning).
thesis: An interactive German explainer of a paper (framed via Integrated Information Theory) that asks why spatial experience feels the way it does: not 'why do we see certain objects' but 'why does the canvas itself feel extended'; it introduces 'spots' (indistinguishable regions of experienced space), argues space is chosen over colour because it is introspectively decomposable and universal, derives extendedness from connection/fusion/inclusion, states the 5 axioms of experience and a central thesis, and models experience on a grid substrate whose inhomogeneities become 'stars in the sky'.
key_claims: The central question is reframed from 'why do we see certain objects' to 'why does the extended canvas itself feel extended' — spatial experience is modelled as a 'painting' whose surface, not just its content, is what we feel.

Space is the right place to start (rather than, e.g., colour) because it is introspectively decomposable (has internal structure), is universal (visual + bodily + ...), and is scientifically accessible.
A 'spot' is any distinguishable region of experienced space, from a tiny point to the whole visual field; space exists even with no objects in it (the empty night sky still feels extended).
Extendedness is derived from three primitive relations: Connection (Verbindung), Fusion (Verschmelzung), and Inclusion (Einschluss); from these, further spatial properties are derived.
The framework is grounded in Integrated Information Theory (IIT): the 5 axioms of experience are the basis, and the theory is used to explain why experience has the structure it does.

Experience is modelled on a grid (Gitter) substrate with connections between nodes; the 'unfolded structure' of the grid and a comparison against a random network show the grid is the right substrate (it yields the right kind of spatial structure that a random net does not).

Inhomogeneities in the grid correspond to 'stars in the sky' (features of experience), and 'attention' is modelled as a gain-increase on some connections; the piece distinguishes a genuine inhomogeneity (a feature) from attention (a modulation of gain), and derives four testable predictions (space needs no 'fire'; changing connections distorts space; a lesion makes space disappear; extending the grid extends space).

internal_tensions: The core tension is between the felt, all-pervasive extension of experience and a discrete grid substrate — the piece has to show that a grid of connected nodes reproduces the continuous 'canvas' feel, and it uses the grid-vs-random-network contrast to argue the grid is special.

title: Heidegger: Was heißt Denken? — Interactive Explorer
category_reason: Philosophie: interaktive Erkundung von Heideggers Vorlesungsreihe 'Was heißt Denken?' (1951–52): Vierfach-Frage, Nietzsche (die Wüste wächst, Übermensch, ewige Wiederkehr), Parmenides-Spruch, griechische Termini, die Zwiefalt. Keine ML-/KI-Inhalte.
thesis: Heideggers Vorlesungsreihe 'Was heißt Denken?' dreht sich um eine scheinbar simple Frage, die sich als die tiefste der heutigen Zeit erweist: Denken ist kein Wissenschafts-Betrieb, sondern das Antwort-Bereitsein auf den 'Geheiß' (Geheiß), der uns ins Denken beruft – und dieses 'Was' ist die Zwiefalt (das Zu-sammen von Sein und Seiendem), der ungedachte Grund aller westlichen Metaphysik.
key_claims: Die Vierfach-Frage: (1) Was heißt das Wort 'Denken'? (2) Was versteht die Tradition unter Denken? (3) Was müssen wir mitbringen, um richtig zu denken? (4) Was ruft uns ins Denken? – die vierte ist die regierende Frage.

'Die Wissenschaft denkt nicht': Wissenschaften arbeiten in vorgegebenen Bereichen (Natur, Geschichte, Sprache), können aber deren Wesen nicht questionieren – zwischen Denken und Wissenschaft klafft eine Lücke, keine Brücke.

Teil I liest Nietzsche als letzten Metaphysiker: 'Die Wüste wächst', der letzte Mensch (blinzeln), der Übermensch (Übergang, kein Supermensch), der Geist der Rache, die ewige Wiederkehr des Gleichen als Gipfel des westlichen Denkens.

Teil II kehrt zum Parmenides-Spruch zurück: 'χρή τό λέγειν τε νοεῖν τ' ἐόν ἔμμεναι' – Heidegger übersetzt es nicht als 'Man muss sagen und denken, dass das Seiende ist', sondern 'Es braucht: das Vor-legen, so auch das Ein-herz-nehmen: das Seiende im Sein'.

Die Zwiefalt (Zwiefalt): das Wort ἐόν benennt zugleich 'ein Seiendes' und 'Sein' (das Präsenz) – dieses Zu-sammen, das nie selbst questioniert wurde, ist der ungedachte Grund aller Metaphysik (Plato → Kant → Hegel).

Griechische Termini (λέγειν, νοεῖν, ἐόν, ἀλήθεια, φύσις, μετοχή) müssen in ihrer ursprünglichen Resonanz gehört werden, bevor sie durch lateinische Übersetzung und moderne Benutzung abgeflacht wurden.

Denken ist 'Handwerk' (Hand-Werk): das einfachste und deshalb schwerste Handwerk des Menschen – der Denker muss dem entsprechen, was sich zu denken gibt, wie der Schreiner den im Holz schlafenden Formen.

title: Was heißt Denken? — Interactive Visual Exploration
category_reason: Interactive visualization of Heidegger's 'What Is Called Thinking?' (the four questions, the Twofold, Nietzsche, Parmenides); philosophy/phenomenology, no ML
thesis: A visually playful unpacking of Heidegger's Was heißt Denken (GA 8, 1951–52): the question of thinking splits into four modes, and what most calls for thinking withdraws while drawing us toward it — explored through the withdrawal paradox, Nietzsche's bridge over revenge, Parmenides' Geheiß, and the unthought Twofold of beings and Being.
key_claims: The question 'what is thinking?' unfolds into four: (1) what the word 'thinking' (Gedank) means; (2) what tradition has taken thinking to be (logic, λόγος, judgment); (3) what we must bring to think (a leap/readiness, not a method); (4) what calls us to think — the decisive, most thought-provoking question

title: Whitehead's Prozessphilosophie – Interaktiv
category_reason: An interactive canvas embodying Whitehead's process philosophy (actual occasions, prehension, concrescence); no machine-learning subject.
thesis: An interactive canvas embodiment of Whitehead's process philosophy: each glowing particle is an 'Actual Occasion' — born, prehends its surroundings, concresces toward a subjective aim, satisfies, and perishes, leaving 'objective immortality' as data for new occasions.
key_claims: Reality is made of Actual Occasions (drops of experience), not enduring substances.
Each occasion has a life cycle: birth -> prehension (feeling) -> concrescence (becoming) -> satisfaction -> perishing.
Prehension = an occasion 'feels' others (range and strength sliders draw connecting lines).

Subjective Aim = an inner goal (high -> ordered motion, low -> chaotic drift); Eternal Objects = pure possibilities (colors/forms); Creativity = the drive to produce new occasions; God = an ordering principle (order vs chaos).
Perished occasions live on as data ('objective immortality') that can seed influenced child occasions.
methods_math: qualitative particle dynamical system (aim-attractor force, neighbor prehension, stochastic creativity noise, damping)
visualizations: canvas particle system: Actual Occasions with glow, trails, phase rings, prehension lines to neighbors, ghost 'objective immortality' traces, mouse hover tooltip, click-to-spawn creativity burst, presets (chaos/harmony/creative/contemplative) that animate the sliders
seven sliders: Creativity, Prehension range, Prehension strength, Aim, Eternal Objects, Concrescence, God/order
internal_tensions: An aesthetic simulation — the sliders are pedagogical metaphors, not a rigorous model of process philosophy.
'God as ordering principle' reduces Whitehead's dipolar God to a simple center-pulling harmonic attractor.

title: What is Wisdom?
category_reason: A self-help / practical-philosophy interactive on the nature of wisdom; no math or ML involved.
thesis: Wisdom is not knowledge but knowing when to act and when to walk away; it lives in balance between opposites (courage/caution) and is a practice built from five pillars (self-awareness, long-term thinking, empathy, comfort with uncertainty, learning from pain) — the quiet voice that says 'wait' when everything screams 'go'.
key_claims: Wisdom != knowledge: knowing fire is hot is knowledge; knowing when to use fire and when to walk away is wisdom.

Wisdom 'holds the tension between extremes' — a balance slider shows all-caution (fear disguised as prudence) vs all-impulse (confidence without awareness = recklessness), with the sweet spot holding both courage and caution.

Five pillars: Self-Awareness (seeing clearly vs. what you want to see), Long-term Thinking (right over easy, 'the marshmallow test of life every day'), Empathy (people as whole, not roles), Comfort with Uncertainty (saying 'I don't know' without panic), Learning from Pain (reflection, not suffering, creates wisdom).

Wisdom vs. not-wisdom contrasts: listening to understand vs. speaking to prove smart; responding from clarity vs. reacting from emotion; wanting to understand vs. needing to be right; living one truth deeply vs. collecting unused advice.
'Suffering does not automatically create wisdom; reflection on suffering does — the scar becomes a teacher only if you listen.'
visualizations: pure JS interactive: scroll-reveal cards, a courage/caution balance slider with 5 banded messages, a 'spot the wiser response' choice with feedback, 5 click-to-reveal pillars, a wisdom-vs-not comparison grid, and a final-insight reveal with a progress bar
internal_tensions: It is normative self-help that treats 'wisdom' as a single coherent virtue with 5 fixed pillars; it offers no definition rigorous enough to test, and the 'wise' vs 'learning' choice labels quietly privilege one response (pause over react).

title: Raum, Zug und kohaerente Verschiedenheit
category_reason: A philosophical 'worldview' essay arguing that the train, word-embeddings, HoTT, sheaves and Schmitz all instantiate one idea — coherent difference — with AI only one illustration among several.
thesis: Maybe space is not the fundamental thing; 'coherent difference' is. An object (the train, a word's meaning, an equality in HoTT, a sheaf) is not a hidden central thing behind its perspectives but the very network of coherences between them — and that same structure recurs across perception, AI embeddings, homotopy type theory, and sheaf theory.
key_claims: You can never point to a single sensation and say 'that is the train'; the train is what it is that all the senses (seeing, hearing, feeling, locating) cohere / fit together without contradicting.

The classical answer — there is a central thing (Ding) behind the perspectives — is challenged: the center can be removed and the coherence structure remains (marked as a mere equivalence, 'nur Kohaerenz').
The same move happens in AI: a language model does not know what 'Katze' is, only where it sits in a relation network; meaning = position in the relation network, not a property of the word.
HoTT: equality a=b is not primitive yes/no but a space of paths, with homotopies between paths ad infinitum — again a space of connections, not a single identity.
Sheaves: local data over open sets that agree on overlaps glue into a global object — local coherence produces the global.
Conclusion: space is just the most immediate form in which we can see coherent difference (as nearness, farness, direction, path).
visualizations: interactive SVG/HTML scenes: clickable senses, a centered graph whose center can be removed (becoming a centerless coherence net), a word-embedding space (Katze/Hund/... vs Quasar/Galaxie), a click-to-draw paths-between-a-and-b HoTT canvas, and a 6-card 'map' (Zug/KI/HoTT/Schmitz/Garbe/Kern) showing the correspondences
internal_tensions: The unifying claim ('all is the same structure') is explicitly a philosophical thesis, not a formal result — the file itself calls it a 'gemeinsame strukturelle Linse' (common structural lens), not an established ontology.

It treats sheaf gluing, HoTT identity types, and embedding geometry as literally the same thing, erasing real formal differences (sheaf equality is strict, HoTT equality is identity types, embeddings are metrical).

title: Étale Raum & Étale Kohomologie — visuell
category_reason: Pure algebraic geometry / number theory (étale cohomology, Weil conjectures, ℓ-adic cohomology); no AI application.
thesis: A visual tour of étale space and étale cohomology: the étale space of a sheaf (stalks over the base), étale morphisms as algebraic (unbranched) coverings, the étale site (a Grothendieck topology), Čech cohomology (gluing on overlaps), and the payoff — ℓ-adic cohomology and Frobenius eigenvalues behind the Weil conjectures / Deligne's Riemann hypothesis over finite fields.
key_claims: The étale space Ét(F) is the disjoint union of stalks F_x; a section is a continuous section of the projection pi, which is a local homeomorphism (hence 'étale').
An étale morphism = flat + unbranched = a local-homeomorphism analogue that works in positive characteristic (e.g. z -> z^n on C*).
The étale site replaces open sets by étale morphisms with surjective étale families as covers — a Grothendieck topology that needs no points.
Čech cohomology measures how local sections fail to glue to global ones; the cocycle condition dc=0 (e.g. c_23 - c_13 + c_12 = 0 mod 4).
Étale cohomology gives finite-dimensional Q_l spaces with a Frobenius action; #X(F_{q^n}) = sum (-1)^i tr(Frob^n | H^i_et); Deligne showed |eigenvalue| = q^{i/2} (Riemann over finite fields).
Comparison theorem: for smooth X/C, H^i_et(X, Z/n) is isomorphic to the singular cohomology H^i(X(C), Z/n).
methods_math: Frobenius action / Weil conjectures / Lefschetz trace formula
visualizations: canvas étale space (base line X, vertical stalks, a section running on one sheet, sheet-count slider + 'wiggle section')
canvas covering z -> z^n (base circle, n preimages, monodromy rotation toggle, degree slider)
canvas étale site (add surjective étale 'covers' drawn as multi-sheet arcs over X)
canvas Čech: three overlapping open sets U1,U2,U3 on S^1, click to cycle 1-cochain values in Z/4, toggle the cocycle check (check/cross + status)
canvas Frobenius eigenvalues (elliptic-curve-style spectrum, q=5; weight circles 1, sqrt(q), q; Frob^n slider -> Lefschetz sum)
MathJax-rendered formulas throughout
internal_tensions: Visual/metaphorical — 'étale site covers' drawn as arcs is an analogy; the real object is a category with a coverage notion.
The Frobenius widget is one specific toy (q=5, a single elliptic-curve-like spectrum), not a general computation.
